risk_of_bias.note: The cohort is at very high risk of bias on its card (ROBINS-E): with no comparison group, the drug cannot be separated from the ceremony's setting, group, ritual, teaching and expectations; about 85 in 100 baseline respondents are missing from the paired analyses, with no comparison of those who stayed and those who left; analytic samples differ between analyses and are not stated; the path model kept significant predictors only; and the questionnaire is new and self-rated, in a culture where the expected direction is familiar. The survey selected respondents on the outcome and asked them to recall earlier beliefs years later (JBI: high risk). The trial is randomized, but its belief items are a 5-item version without reported reliability, analysed secondarily with one-tailed tests, and the paper does not say whether patients could tell their treatment.

inconsistency.note: The direction agrees across the cohort, the trial and the survey (away from materialism, towards panpsychism and wider attribution of consciousness); the conversion tables also show moves towards materialism, which the statement reports. The two papers differ on the role of mystical experience (no link in the cohort's path model, a link in the survey), which the statement also reports.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded, for self-selected ceremony attendees, patients in one trial and survey respondents chosen for a belief change; the statement does not extend the shifts to people who use psychedelics in general.

imprecision.note: The cohort's shifts exclude no change (editors' approximate 95% intervals for d 0.15 to 0.51 at 4 weeks and 0.27 to 0.65 at 6 months); the trial's difference between arms is imprecise (two-sided p about 0.08), which the statement says.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable: no registration or analysis plan is mentioned for the cohort or the survey analyses, and the paper does not say whether the belief items were a registered outcome of the trial.

rate.reasoning: Observational evidence (a prospective cohort without a comparison group and a retrospective survey) starts low; rated down two levels for risk of bias, which is below the floor: very low. Rated as worded: an association between attending a psychedelic ceremony and modest shifts in stated beliefs among people who kept answering; not that psychedelics cause the shift, that it is specific to psychedelics (escitalopram also moved, d = 0.2, and the difference between the arms was significant only one-tailed), or that it lasts beyond 6 months. The trial is randomized and would start high on its own, but as the only comparison between treatments it rests on 59 patients, a 5-item version and a one-tailed p of 0.041 (about 0.08 two-sided), so it qualifies the claim rather than raising it. Status replicated by the same team: the cohort and the trial are one group's two samples, reported in one paper; the survey from another group agrees in direction but recruited people because their beliefs had changed and relied on recall, so it is not counted as an independent test. Whether the beliefs are true is outside what any of these designs can address, as both teams say.
rate.population: Adults who planned to attend a retreat, ceremony or other guided experience with a classic psychedelic and signed up at a study website after online advertisements (819 in the baseline table: mean age 44.4; 55.6% men; 43.8% from the United States and 19.5% from the United Kingdom; 90.7% White; 54.1% with a master's, doctoral or professional degree, editors' sum), of whom 122 answered the belief questions at baseline, 4 weeks and 6 months; 59 adults with major depression (30 and 29) in a randomized trial by the same team; and 1,606 adults recruited online by another team because they attributed a change in their beliefs to a psychedelic experience (mean age 35.1; 67% men; 89% White; 69% from the United States).
rate.exposure: Attending a ceremony or retreat with a classic psychedelic (psilocybin mushrooms or truffles, ayahuasca, DMT, San Pedro, LSD or 1P-LSD), the substance, amount and setting chosen by the respondents and not reported; in the trial, psilocybin therapy: 25 mg on two dosing days and 6 weeks of daily placebo (study condition); in the survey, a past experience with psilocybin mushrooms (49%), LSD (33%), ayahuasca (7%), N,N-DMT (6%), 5-MeO-DMT (3%) or mescaline-containing cacti (2%), chosen by each respondent as the one that most changed their beliefs.
rate.comparator: Each respondent's own answers about a week before the ceremony (no comparison group); in the trial, randomized daily escitalopram for 6 weeks with two 1 mg doses of psilocybin; in the survey, respondents' remembered 'before' beliefs, rated in the same sitting as 'after' and 'now'.
rate.outcome: Agreement with non-physicalist statements: a 9-item factor (Cronbach's alpha 0.86) of a 13-item Metaphysical Beliefs Questionnaire written for the study, and 5 of its items in the trial; fatalistic determinism (FAD-Plus items); changes in the position most strongly endorsed; in the survey, the share agreeing that ten kinds of entity can be conscious, five superstition items and one free-will item. Whether any belief is true was not assessed.
rate.magnitude: Timmermann et al. (2021), cohort, 122 with paired data: non-physicalist factor at 4 weeks t(121) = 3.66, Bonferroni p = 0.001, d = 0.33; at 6 months t(121) = 5.07, p < 0.0001, d = 0.46 (the printed 95% CIs [0.12, 0.39] and [0.22, 0.50] cannot be intervals of d; editors' approximate 95% intervals for d, SE = √(1/n + d²/2n), 0.15 to 0.51 and 0.27 to 0.65); first-timers (53): d = 0.53 and 0.73; fatalistic determinism d = 0.25 at 4 weeks (p = 0.012), not at 6 months. Conversion (Figure 2; group sizes not printed): 'hard materialists' remaining 24.4% (4 weeks) and 22.2% (6 months); dualists remaining 55.5% and 65.2%; none/mixed to materialism 17.6% and 15.2%; panpsychism neutral to believer 57.3% and 54.5%, sceptic to believer 22.6% and 37.8%. Lifetime psychedelic use and baseline factor score: Spearman r = 0.223 (cross-sectional). Path model: emotional synchrony to the 4-week score, beta 0.22. Trial (psilocybin therapy 30, escitalopram 29; 5 items): interaction F(56) = 3.13, p = 0.041 one-tailed (editors' calculation: two-sided p = 0.082); psilocybin Z = 2.28, p = 0.02, d = 0.45; escitalopram Z = 0.24, p = 0.33, d = 0.2 (Z = 0.24 gives a one-tailed p of about 0.41, editors' calculation). Nayak & Griffiths (2022), 1,606, % agreeing before, after and now: plants 26, 61, 64; fungi 21, 56, 62; insects 33, 57, 60; inanimate natural objects 8, 26, 29; inanimate man-made objects 3, 15, 17; the universe 34, 80, 82; self 80, 97, 98; no meaningful change for superstitions (black cats 8, 4, 3; Loch Ness monster 10, 10, 10) or free will (74, 74, 73).
rate.short: These studies can't say if it's the truth. But beliefs do shift a bit, towards ideas like other worlds and a conscious universe. The shift was still there 6 months later.
rate.rate: Mostly one study with no comparison group, where most people stopped answering, plus a small trial and a survey of people chosen because their beliefs had changed. None can say whether the beliefs are true.

risk_of_bias.note: The estimates are before-and-after changes in self-ratings: the parent trials' randomization does not protect them (RoB 2 high on the MacLean card), and the patient study has no control group (ROBINS-I critical). The volunteers could probably tell when they had the high dose, were unpaid, motivated and mostly spiritually active, and their expectations were not measured; the mystical-experience groups were formed by what happened in the session; the patients knew they had psilocybin, their depression was lifting, and their extreme baseline scores leave room for regression towards the norms. MacLean et al. describe every high-dose session as blinded, but the 2006 report, as its checked card gives it, says 6 of its 36 volunteers had open-label psilocybin in a third session, and MacLean's 35 Study 1 volunteers would include at least five of them (editors' inference).

inconsistency.note: In the trial that supplied 35 of the 52 volunteers, the randomized comparison found no difference in any personality factor (no values printed), while the pooled within-person analysis found a rise in Openness; and the two papers disagree on whether the change followed the experience (mystical score r = 0.42 in the volunteers; no peak-experience score related to Openness in the patients). Small groups and different designs may explain part of this; nothing resolves it.

indirectness.note: The question is whether psilocybin changes personality; the evidence is self-ratings only, with no behaviour and no ratings of personality by others, in selected volunteers (high baseline Openness, spiritually active) and in patients with treatment-resistant depression, in supported clinical or laboratory settings.

imprecision.note: 52 and 19 people; the main change has p = 0.023 and the lasting change p = 0.0503 in a subgroup of 30; a few large individual rises carry much of the mean (about +1.3 without the three largest, editors' approximate calculation); the randomized comparison prints no values, so its precision cannot be judged.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable: neither paper mentions a registration or analysis plan; the 2006 trial did publish its null personality result.

rate.reasoning: The personality estimates are before-and-after changes within the same people, not comparisons between randomized conditions, so they are rated as observational and start low; rated down two levels for risk of bias and one each for inconsistency, indirectness and imprecision, which is below the floor: very low. Worded as insufficient evidence on whether psilocybin changes personality: that self-rated Openness was a few points higher after than before in these two samples is reported in the statement, not rated as an effect of the drug. Counted once: the 2006 trial supplied 35 of MacLean's 52 volunteers, so its null comparison and MacLean's rise come largely from the same people; the patient study is from a London team that includes MacLean's first author, and its Openness rise points the same way under different conditions. Status contested: the before-and-after rises point one way, and the one randomized comparison, the subgroup on which the lasting change rests and the two papers' disagreement about the experience point the other; the debate box sets out both sides. Neither paper checked a change against behaviour.
rate.population: 52 healthy, hallucinogen-naive, unpaid volunteers recruited by community flyers for a study of states of consciousness brought about by psilocybin (35 from a 2006 trial and 17 from a 2011 trial at Johns Hopkins; mean age 46; 22 men and 30 women, editors' sum; 54% with postgraduate degrees; 90% regularly taking part in religious services, discussion groups, prayer or meditation; screening Openness T 65.4 and 62.7); in the 2006 trial, 30 volunteers randomized to drug order (15 per order); and 19 analysed of 20 adults with moderate to severe treatment-resistant unipolar depression in an open-label study in London (6 women, 13 men; mean age 44.7; five had tried a psychedelic before).
rate.exposure: Psilocybin by mouth with preparation and support, as study conditions only: one session at 30 mg/70 kg (in the 2011 trial within four ascending or descending doses with a placebo session), lying down with an eye mask and music, after at least 8 hours of meetings with the session monitors; in the open-label study, 10 mg and then 25 mg a week later, eyes closed with music and two therapists, with integration visits afterwards.
rate.comparator: Each person's own personality scores before (screening or baseline), with no concurrent comparison of change in either main study; within the healthy volunteers, people with and without a 'complete mystical experience' (not randomized) and, separately, change after a first session of placebo, methylphenidate or psilocybin 5 mg/70 kg; in the 2006 trial, people given psilocybin first against people given methylphenidate first (randomized; no values printed).
rate.outcome: Self-rated personality on the NEO Personality Inventory-Revised (240 items; five domains of six facets; T scores from combined-sex norms), 1 to 2 months after the session and about 14 months after the last session (a mean of 16 months after the high-dose session) in the healthy volunteers, and 3 months after in the patients; no behavioural measure and no ratings of personality by others.
rate.magnitude: MacLean et al. (2011), 52 volunteers, screening to 1–2 months: Openness +2.8 T points, F(1, 51) = 5.47, p = 0.023, partial eta squared 0.10 (editors' calculation: within-person standardized change about 0.32, √(5.47/52)); Neuroticism −0.5 (p = 0.62), Extroversion +0.8 (p = 0.38), Agreeableness +1.7 (F = 2.31, printed p = 0.16; 0.13 by the editors' calculation), Conscientiousness −0.9 (p = 0.28). After a first session without high-dose psilocybin (30): F(1, 29) = 0.52, p = 0.48. Complete mystical experience (30) against not (22): F(1, 50) = 9.32, p = 0.004; +5.7 (t(29) = 3.44, p = 0.002) against −1.2 (t(21) = 0.87, p = 0.39). Mystical score and Openness change r = 0.42, p = 0.002 (editors' 95% CI about 0.17 to 0.62, Fisher z). Follow-up (mean 16 months): complete group +4.2, F(1, 29) = 4.17, p = 0.050 (0.0503 by the editors' calculation); others (21) −0.3, p = 0.86; all participants not reported. Figure 1 (editors' reading): changes from about −12 to +36, about 17 of 51 visible points below zero; about +1.3 without the three largest (editors' approximate calculation). Griffiths et al. (2006, card): no personality factor differed between order groups (15 and 15) at 2 months; no values. Erritzoe et al. (2018), 19 patients, baseline to 3 months (T scores): Neuroticism 76.6 to 70.9 (−5.7, p = 0.002), Extraversion 31.1 to 37.6 (+6.5, p < 0.001), Openness 52.7 to 57.6 (+4.9, p = 0.012), Agreeableness 46.8 to 46.7 (p = 0.953), Conscientiousness 29.9 to 33.1 (+3.2, p = 0.086); printed d −0.571, 0.716, 0.437, −0.006 and 0.273, from a formula whose denominator is not divided by 2 (about 0.71 times the usual average-SD d; editors' calculation); Openness change in responders (7) against non-responders (12) 11 ± 21 against 7 ± 6, p = 0.623 (units not stated); insightfulness with Neuroticism change r = −0.47 (p = 0.043) and with Extraversion change r = 0.54 (p = 0.017), uncorrected; no peak-experience score related to the Openness change.
rate.short: Not proven. After psilocybin, people rated themselves about 3 to 5 points more 'open' 1 to 3 months later, on a scale where the average adult scores 50.
rate.rate: Two small before-and-after studies of selected volunteers and patients rating themselves. The one test against another drug found no difference. Both sides are below.

risk_of_bias.note: No validated instrument exists for a theoretical model; on the card's checklist the comparison with hallucinations is high risk: it is by eye, against a few drawings redrawn from secondary sources (popular-science articles, a petroglyph, cave-art illustrations), with no measure of fit; two premises have no source (that all observers report Klüver's form constants, and the 30 to 40 repetitions that set the expected scale); and the results are sensitive to the assumed lateral connectivity, the contour-forming patterns appearing only with lateral spread wider than the anatomy that motivated the model. The mathematics itself is printed in full.

inconsistency.note: One model; no competing model is developed or compared.

indirectness.note: No measurement in people, and none during drug use: the drug enters only as an abstract rise in excitability or fall in inhibition, the same mechanism the paper offers for flickering light, and the anatomy comes mainly from cats, macaques, owl monkeys and tree shrews (partly unpublished), scaled to human V1.

publication_bias.note: Not applicable to a single theoretical paper.

rate.reasoning: A theoretical model is not evidence from measurement and starts low; rated down one level for risk of bias (the fit to hallucinations judged by eye against a few redrawn images, unsourced premises, sensitivity to the assumed connectivity) and one for indirectness (no human or drug data; the drug as an abstract parameter; animal anatomy), which is below the floor: very low. Worded as insufficient evidence on whether psychedelic geometric visuals arise this way: what the model proposes, what it rests on and what it predicts are reported as such, not rated as findings about the brain. Status single study: one modelling paper; it extends the corresponding author's earlier model (Ermentrout & Cowan, 1979), which is not counted as independent support, and no empirical test of its predictions has been read.
rate.population: No participants: a mathematical model of human primary visual cortex (V1), built from anatomical and physiological findings in cats, macaques, owl monkeys and tree shrews (partly unpublished, cited as personal communications) and from estimates of human V1 size and hypercolumn spacing, and compared with published drawings and descriptions of geometric hallucinations.
rate.exposure: In the model, a rise in network excitability (stronger global coupling, or a steeper neural response through a steady input) or a fall in local inhibition, which the authors describe as one possible effect of hallucinogens and also apply to flickering light; no drug, receptor or dose is modelled.
rate.comparator: The model's uniform resting state, and the earlier Ermentrout–Cowan model without orientation tuning; for the hallucinations, comparison by eye with a few drawings.
rate.outcome: Which repeating (doubly periodic) patterns of V1 activity can emerge when the resting state becomes unstable, which of them are stable, and what they would look like in the visual field after an inverse retinocortical map; resemblance to Klüver's four classes of form constants, judged by eye.
rate.magnitude: No statistical estimates. Retinocortical map constants w0 = 0.087 and epsilon = 0.051 (estimated from Drasdo, 1977); orientation preference repeating about every 300 µm in cat V1 and 0.5 mm in macaque V1; 20% of lateral connections ending on inhibitory cells; human V1 about 3,500 mm² per hemisphere, hypercolumn spacing about 1.33–2 mm, about 1,300 hypercolumns; critical wavelength given as about 2.66 mm (2π × 0.400 / qc at qc = 1 gives 2.51 mm, editors' calculation); 30–40 repetitions around the visual field for commonly reported hallucinations (unsourced), corresponding to 2.4–3.2 mm in V1; contour-forming (even) patterns need lateral spread beyond 45 degrees (theta0 > π/4).
rate.short: Maybe the visual brain's own wiring. A maths model shows how tunnels, spirals, cobwebs and honeycombs could arise there. It wasn't tested in people on a drug.
rate.rate: One maths model, built on brain wiring measured mostly in animals and checked by eye against a few drawings. It wasn't tested against brain activity in people on a drug.

risk_of_bias.note: Registered, randomized, counterbalanced, double-dummy crossover with all 28 analysed (card sc_holze_2022: RoB 2 some concerns). People named the right drug in most sessions (editors' calculation from the printed percentages), and every subjective outcome, including the duration, which is modelled from self-ratings, was rated by people who often knew which drug they had; sequence generation and concealment are not described; most statistics are in an unread supplement; three printed values are impossible. Blood pressure, heart rate and temperature are objective.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: pure psilocybin in capsules and LSD in solution, single study doses, healthy screened volunteers with little drug experience in a hospital room, which the statement says. It claims nothing about mushrooms, other doses or settings, and gives no matching amounts.

imprecision.note: 28 people. The duration difference is large and its test decisive, but 'no difference in kind' rests on non-significant post hoc tests without equivalence margins, and the peak values and statistics for subjective, cardiovascular and adverse effects are in the unread supplement, so their size and spread cannot be checked.

rate.reasoning: Randomized, counterbalanced within-person comparison: starts high (METHODS 6.3). Risk of bias −1 (self-ratings under weak blinding between the two drugs, statistics held in the supplement, impossible printed values) and imprecision −1 (28 people; sameness in kind cannot be shown without equivalence testing) give low. The duration difference on its own (about 9 to 11 hours against 6 to 7, in the same people, with a decisive test and a plausible link to the half-lives) would be rated moderate, held down only by the self-rated outcome; the statement that the experiences were alike in kind would be rated low or lower, and is worded as not shown either way. Status single study: the first within-person comparison, from one laboratory. The authors' dose-equivalence figures rest on doses not given in this study and are not used; no comparison of strength is made.
rate.population: 28 healthy, screened adults (14 women, 14 men; mean age 35, range 25 to 52), recruited by word of mouth or from a pool of people interested in psychedelic trials, and paid; 14 had used a psychedelic before and 10 had never used an illicit drug other than cannabis; excluded were a personal or first-degree family history of major psychiatric disorder, interfering medicines and more than 10 lifetime uses of illicit drugs (cannabis excepted); Basel
rate.exposure: Single oral doses of LSD base as a solution, labelled 100 and 200 µg (analysed content 84.5 µg per 100 µg unit), given double-blind and double-dummy in a calm hospital room with one investigator, in random, counterbalanced order with at least 10 days between sessions (study conditions)
rate.comparator: Psilocybin 15 and 30 mg in capsules (analysed 4.61 mg per 5 mg capsule) and placebo, in the same people on other days
rate.outcome: Duration and onset of self-rated effects (modelled from 'any drug effect' ratings); peak self-ratings on visual analogue scales, the 5D-ASC (primary outcome, rated at 24 hours), mystical-experience and mood scales; blood pressure, heart rate, body temperature and pupil size; complaint scores for 0 to 12 and 12 to 24 hours and adverse events within 48 to 72 hours; guesses of which drug was given
rate.magnitude: Holze et al. (2022), 28 people. Table 1 (mean ± SD, range; psilocybin 15 mg, psilocybin 30 mg, LSD 100 µg, LSD 200 µg): effect duration 5.6 ± 2.2 (2.5–10), 6.5 ± 2.4 (3.7–12), 9.3 ± 3.2 (5.7–17) and 11 ± 3.7 (5.4–20) h, F(3,81) = 34.4, p < 0.001, both LSD doses longer than both psilocybin doses (p < 0.001); time to onset 0.8 ± 0.3, 0.8 ± 0.4, 0.6 ± 0.2 and 0.4 ± 0.2 h, F(3,81) = 12.5 (LSD 100 µg different only from psilocybin 30 mg, p < 0.05; LSD 200 µg from both, p < 0.001). Peak subjective effects: psilocybin 30 mg against either LSD dose, no significant difference on any visual analogue scale or 5D-ASC subscale; LSD 200 µg against psilocybin 30 mg different only on MEQ ineffability; both LSD doses higher than psilocybin on AMRS emotional excitation (statistics in unread Supplementary Tables S1–S4). Autonomic (direction and significance from the text; approximate peaks of the group mean curves read from Fig. 3, not the per-person maxima analysed): systolic about 139 (psilocybin 30 mg), 134 (15 mg), 131–133 (LSD) and 118–120 mmHg (placebo); diastolic about 88, 84, 80–81 and 73–74 mmHg; heart rate about 81–82 (LSD 200 µg), 76–77 (LSD 100 µg), 72 (psilocybin 30 mg), 67–68 (15 mg) and 62–65 bpm (placebo); temperature about 37.65 (psilocybin 30 mg), 37.3–37.4 (other active conditions) and 36.7 °C (placebo). Complaints: acute (0–12 h) scores raised by all four active conditions against placebo, subacute (12–24 h) by LSD 200 µg and psilocybin 30 mg (values in unread Supplementary Table S6). Events within 48 h, by drug (psilocybin, LSD): headache 4 and 3; migraine 0 and 1; nosebleed 1 and 0; low mood 2 and 2; nausea 2 and 1; nightmares 1 and 0; restlessness 1 and 1; vivid dreams 0 and 1; insomnia 1 and 0; involuntary leg movements 0 and 1; flashbacks 9 episodes in 5 people within 72 h (4 after psilocybin, 5 after LSD); no severe adverse events. Half-lives (geometric mean, range): LSD 4.3 (2.5–6.0) and 4.0 (2.3–7.1) h; psilocin 2.4 (1.7–3.1) and 2.7 (1.9–3.4) h. Blinding: placebo identified in 96% of sessions; the given condition named correctly in 64%, 57%, 57% and 61% of sessions; the right drug, either dose, in at least 64%, 86%, 78% and 79% (editors' calculation from the printed percentages).
rate.short: Mostly how long it lasts: about 9 to 11 hours for LSD, 6 to 7 for psilocybin, the drug in mushrooms. Otherwise 28 people in a lab rated the trips alike.
rate.rate: One careful lab study of 28 people, who took both drugs in random order. But most could tell which drug they had, and 'alike' only means no clear difference was found.

risk_of_bias.note: The comparison that carries the claim, MDA against MDMA, is between different people from separate studies, which is why it starts low. On top of that: the unequal recording windows (8 against 6 hours) bear directly on the duration comparison; the MDMA volunteers are not described and their number differs between analyses (16 or 12); MDA and its placebo came on consecutive days with MDA still in the blood the next day; the self-ratings come from experienced volunteers who probably recognised MDA; no registration is reported; computerized tasks, adverse events and the two-week check are not reported (card sc_baggott_2019: RoB 2 high overall; the editors' cross-study domain high). One level, not two, because the heart-rate comparison is objective and the window problem runs against the difference observed (editors' reasoning).

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: one dose of each drug at study doses, in healthy, experienced volunteers in hospital, which the statement says. No comparison of strength is made: the paper's areas under the curve for overall drug effect, high, good effect and liking are not used, because they mix strength with length and the recording windows differed.

imprecision.note: 12 MDA participants and 12 to 16 MDMA participants, no intervals; the heart-rate difference rests on p = 0.03 and the diastolic and prolactin differences on p = 0.06 and 0.07; the differences in kind are F tests in 12 people per drug.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; no trial registration is reported.

rate.reasoning: The MDA–MDMA comparison is across separate studies and not randomized, so it is rated as observational and starts low (METHODS 6.3; brief for round pdf-2026-11-14), although MDA against its own placebo is a within-person, placebo-controlled comparison. Risk of bias −1 and imprecision −1 give very low (the scale stops there). MDA's effects against its own placebo (raised self-ratings, closeness, perceptual changes, heart rate and blood pressure, effects still present at 8 hours) would be rated higher on their own, but the claim is about how MDA differs from MDMA and inherits its weakest necessary link, the cross-study comparison. Status single study: one paper, whose MDMA data come from the same team's earlier studies (not read). Doses are given only as study conditions and no strength comparison is made. The abstract's 'well-tolerated' has no adverse-event data behind it, which the statement says.
rate.population: 12 healthy, screened adult volunteers with earlier self-reported experience of MDA, or of both MDMA and a classic psychedelic such as LSD, and no drug dependence other than nicotine or caffeine (mean age 27.8, SD 8; few women, number not given), studied during one hospital stay in San Francisco; MDMA comparison data from 12 to 16 other volunteers in two earlier studies by the same team, not described in this paper
rate.exposure: One oral dose of racemic MDA, 1.4 mg/kg (83 to 128 mg), in a capsule after a two-hour fast, given double-blind by researchers in hospital (study conditions)
rate.comparator: Placebo in the same 12 people on the day before or after (half in each order; how the order was set is not stated); for the drug comparison, racemic MDMA 1.5 mg/kg and its placebo given to other volunteers in two earlier studies by the same team (not randomized against MDA; self-ratings and heart rate recorded to 6 hours instead of 8)
rate.outcome: Self-rated drug effects over time (visual analogue scales, to 8 hours after MDA and 6 after MDMA); a 66-item altered-states questionnaire rated at 8 hours for the peak; affect and social-feeling scales before and 2.5 hours after dosing; heart rate and blood pressure hourly; unwanted effects as rated (no adverse-event data reported); MDA's half-life in blood
rate.magnitude: Baggott et al. (2019): MDA n = 12; MDMA comparison n = 16 (visual analogue scales) or 12 (altered-states and affect and social scales). Length: at 6 h no MDMA effect significantly above its placebo; MDA raised all five general drug-effect items at 6 h and all except bad drug effect at 8 h; any drug effect at 6 h 41.6 ± 7 points above MDMA (z = 6.3, p < 0.001) and 46.4 ± 7 above placebo (z = 6.7, p < 0.001); at 8 h 35.6 ± 10 above placebo (t = 3.7, p = 0.001); MDMA not recorded beyond 6 h. Altered-states questionnaire (F(3,21), Westfall-corrected pairwise tests, printed in Figure 1): complex imagery 20.6, elementary imagery 13.9, spiritual experience 24.8 (MDA > MDMA; both > placebo); dread of ego dissolution 15.1, impaired control and cognition 11.1, anxiety 5.09 (p = 0.008) (MDMA > MDA; MDMA > placebo; MDA not > placebo); audio-visual synesthesia 8.26 (MDA > placebo only); oceanic boundlessness 35.9, visionary changes 21.3, blissful state 32.4, insightfulness 19.4, changed meaning of percepts 13.1, experience of unity 17.9, disembodiment 10.8 (both > placebo; no difference between the drugs). Closeness to others (area under the curve, mean ± SEM): MDA 168.0 ± 53 against its placebo 11.5 ± 38; MDMA 114.4 ± 44 against its placebo −12.5 ± 16; MDA and MDMA not significantly different (F(3,21) = 5.26, p = 0.0073). Affiliation raised by MDMA only (no statistic printed). Bad drug effect area 47.9 ± 26 (MDA) and 41.4 ± 16 (MDMA), neither significantly above its placebo (F(3,21) = 3.1, p = 0.0487, no significant pairwise difference); anxious F(3,21) = 1.26, p = 0.3116; paranoia F(3,21) = 1.71, p = 0.196. Heart rate rise 20 ± 3 bpm (MDA) against 30.6 ± 4.5 (MDMA), p = 0.03; peak systolic rise 33 ± 2 against 31 ± 3 mmHg; diastolic 24 ± 2 against 19 ± 2 mmHg, p = 0.06 (the ± is not defined in this paragraph); main effects of condition F(3,22) = 17.1 (heart rate), 61.7 (systolic) and 32.4 (diastolic), p < 0.0001. Prolactin rise 16 ± 6 against 29 ± 6 ng/mL (p = 0.07); cortisol 16 ± 1 against 13 ± 2 µg/dL. MDA half-life 10.9 ± 4 h (mean ± SD); the MDMA half-life compared, 8.1 ± 2 h, is from Kolbrich et al. (2008a; 1.6 mg/kg; another team). No adverse-event data reported. The paper's areas under the curve for any drug effect, high, good drug effect and liking are not used here: they mix strength with length, and the recording windows differed.
rate.short: It seemed to last longer, with more visuals and less anxiety: at 6 hours MDA was still clearly felt and MDMA wasn't. That's one small lab study.
rate.rate: One small lab study of 12 people, set beside MDMA results from different people whose results stop sooner. So the differences may come from the people or the timing, not the drugs.

risk_of_bias.note: Measurement and selection within each sample: in Israel an unvalidated retrospective rating scale, an unverified exposure of unknown dose and content, interviews partly by telephone by unnamed interviewers, and no stated recruitment, place or dates (card sc_zemishlany_2001, JBI prevalence checklist: high); in Northern Ireland no description of how the interviews were analysed and no counts behind 'a slight majority', 'some' or 'several' (card sc_mcelrath_2005, editors' qualitative checklist: high). The Israeli table lets every count be checked, so one level.

inconsistency.note: The two studies agree on the kinds of experiences (more desire or closeness; erection and orgasm difficulties for some men; heightened desire for others). They differ on desire: all 35 reported more of it in Israel, while in Northern Ireland a slight majority described closeness rather than desire, which the statement explains, as the editors' reading, by the Israeli sample's selection for use before sex.

indirectness.note: Coverage: neither sample has a sampling frame; the Israeli sample was selected for having used MDMA before sex and the Northern Irish one was reached through agencies, contacts and paid referral; both are from the 1990s, and the author of the second says the scene has probably changed.

imprecision.note: Small samples (20 men, 15 women; 95% intervals about 40 points wide around the sex-specific shares, editors' calculation), stated with the counts; the claim is already at the floor.

rate.reasoning: A descriptive claim, rated as a description of the people sampled (METHODS 6.3): starts low; risk of bias -1 and indirectness -1 give very low, the floor; never upgraded. Status replicated: the Israeli survey and the Northern Irish interviews are independent samples by different teams that agree on the kinds of experiences people describe, not on how often each occurs, which neither can show. Neither study measured sexual function, tested the pills or compared occasions with and without MDMA, so the statement makes no causal claim: what people recalled may reflect the drug, other drugs taken (cannabis for 20 of the 35; alcohol often in Northern Ireland), expectations or the people themselves. The Israeli summary's 'erection impaired in 40%' is given with the other 40% who reported better erections, and the risk accounts are given with the finding that condoms were also rare without drugs. Findings only: nothing here is about choosing or using MDMA for sex.
rate.population: People who had used ecstasy, in two self-selected samples: 35 in Israel (20 men aged 22 to 46, 15 women aged 21 to 48) who had occasionally used MDMA before sex, healthy, medication-free and without sexual or major psychiatric disorders, recruitment not described; 98 current or former users in Northern Ireland interviewed in 1997 and 1998 (69% men; aged 17 to 45; 16% gay or bisexual), recruited through notices, a magazine, agencies, contacts, referral and paid recruiters
rate.exposure: MDMA as ecstasy tablets or pills taken by people's own choice, content and amount unknown and not tested (self-reported; in Israel, cannabis sometimes taken with MDMA by 20 of the 35; in Northern Ireland, alcohol and other drugs often taken in the same episodes)
rate.comparator: Each person's memory of their usual sex without MDMA (Israel); none in Northern Ireland, where respondents compared experiences in their own words
rate.outcome: Recalled sexual desire, erection or lubrication, delay and intensity of orgasm, and satisfaction, each rated from -3 to +3 against usual function (Israel); themes in interviews on sensuality, desire, sexual performance and sexual risk (Northern Ireland)
rate.magnitude: Zemishlany et al. (2001), Table I (20 men, 15 women; counts by the editors from the per-person ratings, which match the text's percentages): desire up 35 of 35, moderately or profoundly 34; satisfaction moderately or profoundly up 32 of 35 (Wilson 95% interval 78% to 97%, editors' calculation), men 18 of 20, women 14 of 15; erection worse 8 of 20 men (22% to 61%; 4 moderately or profoundly), better 8, unchanged 4; lubrication more 12 of 15 women (55% to 93%), less 2, unchanged 1; orgasm delayed 16 of 20 men (58% to 92%) and 6 of 15 women (20% to 64%); no orgasm on MDMA 1 man and 2 women; orgasm more intense 17 of 20 men and 8 of 15 women, less intense 1 man and 3 women; satisfaction +2 or +3 in all 8 men with weaker erections and all 3 people without orgasm; cannabis sometimes with MDMA 10 men and 10 women; interviewed by telephone 9 (printed 25%; 9 of 35 is 26%, editors' calculation). McElrath (2005): 98 interviewed (106, 8 discarded); themes only, no counts ('a slight majority' described sensuality or deep emotions rather than sexual desire).
rate.short: Desire often goes up, erections can go either way, and orgasm often takes longer. In one survey, 8 of 20 men said erections got weaker on MDMA, and 8 stronger.
rate.rate: Two small studies from the 1990s: a survey of 35 people who chose to take part and remembered the past, and interviews without counts. Nobody tested the pills or compared times with and without MDMA.

risk_of_bias.note: Randomized by a balanced Latin square (sequence generation and concealment not described; nine people cannot fill a 4 × 4 square evenly), double-dummy with a masked drink, but the experienced men were likely to recognise the conditions and the blind was not checked; drunkenness and sedation are self-ratings; no registration; cardiovascular and other physiological measures were collected and not reported, Table 1 lists only significant results, and the text goes beyond Table 1 in places (card sc_hernandez_lopez_2002: RoB 2 high overall, driven by selective reporting, which bears more on the unreported outcomes than on those described here). Test scores and blood levels are objective.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: 9 experienced men, one amount of each drug, laboratory tests of symbol matching and reaction time rather than driving or real-life impairment, which the statement says.

imprecision.note: 9 people; no standard deviations or intervals for the test and rating outcomes (means in figures only); the central comparisons, feeling as drunk and test scores falling as far as with alcohol alone, are non-significant differences that cannot show equality (the drunk ratings were numerically higher with both drugs), and the printed peak differences do not agree with one another (editors' check: they imply that MDMA alone differed from placebo by −0.89 and by 0 correct responses).

rate.reasoning: Randomized within-person crossover: starts high (METHODS 6.3). Risk of bias −1 and imprecision −2 give very low. The fall in self-rated sedation with both drugs against alcohol alone, and the changes in blood levels, are significant within-person differences and would be rated higher on their own; the claim's main point, that people felt as drunk and did about as badly on the test at its worst, rests on non-significant comparisons in 9 men. Status single study (the dose-finding pilot and the immune results from the same trial were not read). The claim gives risk facts only.
rate.population: 9 healthy men aged 19 to 36 (mean 23) who had used MDMA recreationally on 5 to 100 occasions (mean 26) and had been drunk before, without past adverse reactions to MDMA or drug dependence other than nicotine (7 smoked), all extensive CYP2D6 metabolizers; recruited by word of mouth and paid; Barcelona
rate.exposure: MDMA 100 mg (racemic, capsule, fasting) with alcohol 0.8 g/kg as vodka and tonic (350 ml drunk over 15 minutes, starting 30 minutes after the capsule), given double-blind and double-dummy in 10-hour outpatient sessions in a quiet room (study conditions, not advice)
rate.comparator: The same men given MDMA with a placebo drink, a placebo capsule with alcohol, and both placebos, one week apart, in an order set by a balanced 4 × 4 Latin square
rate.outcome: Digit symbol substitution test and simple reaction time (impairment as fewer responses or slower times than with placebo), eye-muscle balance (Maddox wing), self-rated sedation and other effects (ARCI) and 23 visual analogue scales including drunken and drowsiness, over 6 to 10 hours; blood MDMA and alcohol; cardiovascular and other physiological measures collected but not reported
rate.magnitude: Hernández-López et al. (2002), 9 men; ANOVA df 3,24 with Tukey tests (Table 1). Sedation (ARCI-PCAG): area alcohol > placebo (p < 0.05) and > combination (p < 0.01), combination not different from placebo or MDMA; peak alcohol > combination (p < 0.05). Drowsiness: area alcohol > placebo and > combination (p < 0.01); peak alcohol > placebo (p < 0.01) and > combination (p < 0.05). Drunken: area and peak raised by alcohol and by the combination against placebo and MDMA (p < 0.01); alcohol against combination not significant; approximate peak ratings about 58 (combination) and 40 mm (alcohol alone), read from Fig. 3. Digit symbol substitution, mean peak differences against placebo: alcohol −5.89 total and −9.0 correct responses, combination −4.89 and −8.11 (peak p < 0.01 for both; alcohol against combination not significant); 6-h area: alcohol against placebo p < 0.01, combination not significant; impairment against placebo lasted 2–3 h with alcohol (from 1 h to 3–4 h) and 1 h with the combination (1–2 h). Reaction decision time, peak: combination against placebo p < 0.05, the only significant pair; the combination's impairment lasted half an hour (1–1.5 h). Euphoria and stimulation scales were raised by MDMA and the combination against placebo and alcohol (not compared here for strength or length). Blood levels (Table 2, mean ± SD; time to peak as median): MDMA peak 231.42 ± 36.20 alone and 260.29 ± 42.22 with alcohol, p = 0.007 (13% higher, the paper's figure), units printed as mg/dl but the assay range is 25–400 ng/ml, so ng/ml is likely; time to peak 1.5 h in both (p = 0.058); area 2447.85 ± 711.81 against 2345.08 ± 838.35, p = 0.471 (headed AUC0–6h, while the methods give AUC0–24h for MDMA, which was sampled only to 10 h). Alcohol peak 124.62 ± 14.94 alone and 105.81 ± 4.99 mg/dl with MDMA, p = 0.004 (15% lower); 6-h area 409.08 ± 24.28 against 371.74 ± 18.67, p < 0.001 (9% lower); time to peak 1.5 against 2 h (p = 0.014). No serious adverse reactions; all 9 completed. Cardiovascular, endocrine and other physiological measures were collected and not reported.
rate.short: Just as drunk, but less sleepy, and about as bad on a test at its worst. Blood MDMA also peaked 13% higher, in a lab study of 9 men.
rate.rate: One small lab study of 9 young men who knew MDMA well, with one amount of each drug. 'Just as drunk' means no clear difference was found, and the heart results were never reported.

risk_of_bias.note: Registered, block-randomized, counterbalanced, double-dummy crossover with complete data (card sc_straumann_2023: RoB 2 some concerns). Blood pressure, heart rate, temperature and drug levels are objective; the unwanted-effect scores and ratings are self-reports under imperfect blinding, allocation concealment is not described, most item-level statistics are in an unread supplement, the paper's three statements on nausea disagree, and the text leaves out LSD's effect on MDMA's levels.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: one pair of doses taken together, healthy screened volunteers with limited drug experience, a calm hospital room, which the statement says; it claims nothing about party settings, other doses or timing, or rare harms.

imprecision.note: 24 people. The rises in blood pressure and heart rate against LSD alone are significant, but the findings that temperature and unwanted effects were no higher, or no lower, than with LSD alone are non-significant comparisons, not shown equivalence, and rare harms such as serotonin toxicity cannot be detected in 24 people.

rate.reasoning: Randomized within-person crossover: starts high (METHODS 6.3). Risk of bias −1 and imprecision −1 give low. The larger blood-pressure and heart-rate rises with both drugs than with LSD alone, objective and significant in the same people, would be rated moderate on their own; the findings on temperature and unwanted effects rest on non-significant tests and are worded as such. Status single study: the first controlled human study of the combination, from one laboratory. The claim leaves out how strong or long the good effects felt, and gives no timing.
rate.population: 24 healthy, screened adults (12 women, 12 men; mean age 30, range 25 to 54), recruited by word of mouth or from a pool of people interested in psychedelic trials, and paid; 12 had used a psychedelic and 9 MDMA before (1 to 13 times); excluded were more than 20 lifetime uses of hallucinogens or MDMA, illicit drug use in the past 2 months (cannabis excepted), a personal or first-degree family history of major psychiatric disorder and interfering medicines; Basel
rate.exposure: MDMA 100 mg (four 25 mg capsules; analysed 25.40 mg each) and LSD base 100 µg (oral solution; analysed content 92.5 µg) taken at the same time, double-blind and double-dummy, in a calm hospital room with one investigator (study conditions)
rate.comparator: LSD 100 µg alone, MDMA 100 mg alone and placebo in the same people, at least 10 days apart, in block-randomized, counterbalanced order
rate.outcome: Peak blood pressure, heart rate, body temperature and pupil size; complaint scores for 0 to 12 and 12 to 24 hours, self-rated bad drug effect, fear and nausea, and adverse events; blood levels of LSD and MDMA over 24 hours
rate.magnitude: Straumann et al. (2023), 24 people (Table 1, mean ± SEM; placebo, MDMA, LSD, LSD + MDMA; F(3,69); Tukey tests): systolic 124 ± 2.4, 148 ± 2.9, 137 ± 2.7 and 150 ± 2.9 mmHg (combination against LSD p < 0.001, against MDMA not significant); diastolic 77 ± 1.7, 89 ± 1.4, 85 ± 1.8 and 90 ± 1.4 (combination against LSD p < 0.05); mean arterial 92, 107, 102 and 109 (combination against LSD p < 0.001); heart rate 77 ± 2.6, 95 ± 3.4, 92 ± 4.5 and 100 ± 3.6 bpm (combination against LSD p < 0.05, against MDMA not significant); rate-pressure product 9290, 13698, 12385 and 14678 mmHg × bpm (combination against LSD p < 0.001); body temperature 37.0 ± 0.05, 37.3 ± 0.07, 37.4 ± 0.06 and 37.5 ± 0.08 °C (combination against LSD not significant, against MDMA p < 0.05; MDMA against LSD not significant); pupil size 6.0, 7.1, 7.0 and 7.2 mm (combination against LSD p < 0.05; n = 23). Complaints: acute (0–12 h) 1.9 ± 1.1, 8.6 ± 1.8, 15 ± 1.9 and 15 ± 2.2 (combination against LSD not significant); subacute (12–24 h) −0.2 ± 0.5, 2.5 ± 0.9, 3.1 ± 1.0 and 5.5 ± 1.4 (combination against LSD not significant, against MDMA p < 0.05). Visual analogue peaks (% of maximum): bad drug effect 0.2, 6.4, 18 and 14 (combination against LSD not significant); fear 0.2, 2.3, 13 and 8.2 (not significant); nausea 1.0, 7.9, 25 and 21 (MDMA lower than LSD, p < 0.001, and than the combination, p < 0.05; LSD against combination not significant). Blood levels (Table 2, geometric mean, 95% CI; paired t-tests): LSD peak 1.9 (1.7–2.1) alone and 2.1 (1.9–2.3) ng/mL with MDMA (p < 0.05); half-life 3.9 (3.5–4.4) and 5.2 (4.6–5.9) h (p < 0.001); AUC∞ 14 (12–17) and 19 (16–22) ng·h/mL (p < 0.01); apparent clearance 6.9 and 5.3 L/h (p < 0.01); time to peak 1.6 h in both. MDMA peak 233 (215–252) alone and 208 (189–228) ng/mL with LSD (p < 0.001); time to peak 2.8 (2.5–3.2) and 3.5 (3.0–4.0) h (p < 0.01); half-life 8.3 and 8.2 h; AUC∞ 3083 and 3068 ng·h/mL (some MDMA-alone values from 23 people). Editors' calculation from the printed means: LSD AUC∞ about 36% higher, MDMA peak about 11% lower. No severe adverse events.
rate.short: Blood pressure and heart rate went higher than on LSD alone, and bad feelings weren't clearly eased. In a lab study of 24 people, top blood pressure was 13 points higher.
rate.rate: One careful lab study of 24 healthy people, with one amount of each drug taken together. The blood pressure results are clear; the rest rests on people's own ratings, and rare dangers can't show up in so few.

risk_of_bias.note: Coverage and measurement could materially change the figures. The seizure series depends on which agencies reported and what they tested, neither of which is described, and on policing priorities, and it is reported only at its first and last quarters (card sc_palamar_2022: JBI, moderate as a description of recorded seizures, high as an indicator of supply). Evidence of counterfeit pill use in deaths depends on how completely death investigators documented pills, which the authors expect to vary within and between jurisdictions, rarely rests on pills known to have been tested, and may have been documented more fully as awareness of counterfeit pills grew, which would inflate the rise (the editors' concern, not tested; card sc_odonnell_2023: JBI moderate).

inconsistency.note: The two record systems agree in direction; they measure different things, and the statement does not compare their sizes.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: records of seizures and of deaths with documented evidence, not the contents of pills sold on the street, which the statement says neither source tested; US only, to 2021.

imprecision.note: Large record sets (hundreds to thousands of seizures a quarter; 106,293 and 54,768 deaths); no intervals are printed, but chance is not the main concern.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for surveillance series; not suspected.

rate.reasoning: Descriptive (counts, shares and their change over time in records): starts low, is never upgraded, and is downgraded one level for risk of bias because coverage and measurement could materially change the figures (see the domain note); inconsistency, indirectness as worded, imprecision and publication bias are not downgraded. Very low. Status replicated: two independent record systems, run by different teams, agree in direction (pills became a larger part of US fentanyl seizures in 2018–2021, and deaths with evidence of counterfeit pills a larger share of overdose deaths in 2019–2021); each figure comes from one source, the two measure different things and their sizes cannot be compared, and O'Donnell et al. cite Palamar et al. without sharing its data. Both are compared first quarter against last quarter, and in both the counts or the total share peaked in mid-2021, which the statement says. The drug-checking study qualifies the claim only by showing that it cannot answer for pills. Nothing here measures the share of street pills that contain fentanyl, how much they hold, or the risk of using a counterfeit pill; the DEA laboratory figures on pill contents that Palamar et al. cite were not read and are not used.
rate.population: Fentanyl-containing drug seizures recorded by law-enforcement agencies taking part in the 33 US High Intensity Drug Trafficking Areas (50 states and the District of Columbia), 2018–2021; unintentional and undetermined-intent drug overdose deaths with a medical examiner or coroner report in 30 US jurisdictions (29 states and the District of Columbia), July 2019 to December 2021, and in 35 jurisdictions in 2021; and samples brought for drug checking at two supervised consumption sites in Vancouver, Canada, 2017–2018
rate.exposure: Pill form, against powder form, among fentanyl-containing seizures; documented evidence of counterfeit pill use among overdose deaths
rate.comparator: The first against the last quarter of each period, with no statistical test of the death-record trend; for 2021, overdose deaths without such evidence in the same jurisdictions; census regions
rate.outcome: Quarterly counts of fentanyl-containing powder and pill seizures, the pill share of pill-plus-powder fentanyl seizures and the number of pills seized; the quarterly share of overdose deaths with evidence of counterfeit pill use, the pill imitated and the drugs listed as causes of death
rate.magnitude: Palamar et al. (2022), HIDTA seizure records, 2018 Q1 against 2021 Q4: fentanyl powder seizures 424 against 1,539 (+263.0%); fentanyl pill seizures 68 against 635 (+833.8%); pill share of pill-plus-powder fentanyl seizures 13.8% against 29.2% (68/492 and 635/2,174, editors' calculation); fentanyl-containing pills seized 42,202 against 2,089,186 (+4,850.4%), about 621 against 3,290 pills per pill seizure (editors' calculation); powder weight 298.2 against 2,416.0 kg (+710.2%). Read from the figures (approximate): powder seizures about 2,050 and pill seizures about 675 at their 2021 Q3 peaks; pills seized about 2.73 million and powder weight about 2,920 kg at their 2021 Q2 peaks; the pill share highest in 2021 Q4. No intervals for the changes; the β coefficients are not defined. O'Donnell et al. (2023), SUDORS, 30 jurisdictions, 106,293 deaths: share with evidence of counterfeit pill use 2.0% (2019 Q3) against 4.7% (2021 Q4), high about 5.1% in 2021 Q2 (read from the figure); West 4.7% against 14.7%; other regions below 4%. 2021, 35 jurisdictions: 2,437 of 54,768 deaths (4.4%); counterfeit oxycodone only 1,346 (55.2%; M-30 pills documented in 889, 66.0%), alprazolam only 415 (17.0%), both 95 (3.9%), unspecified 581 (23.8%) (17.0% and 23.8% editors' calculation); West 55.8% against 16.3% of other deaths; with against without evidence: any illicitly manufactured fentanyl 93.0% against 72.2%, these fentanyls only 41.4% against 19.5%, illicit benzodiazepines 5.3% against 1.4% (17.1% with counterfeit alprazolam only, 18.9% with both, 1.5% with counterfeit oxycodone only). No tests or intervals. Tupper et al. (2018): very few pills tested (no number), no results by form.
rate.short: Yes, in US records to 2021. Overdose deaths with signs of fake pills rose from 2 to about 5 in 100, and to about 15 in 100 in western states.
rate.rate: Big US record sets. But seizures depend on what police target and test, death records likely miss fake pills, more in some places than others, and nobody tested a fair sample of pills.

risk_of_bias.note: A single cross-sectional comparison of groups chosen by programme staff, with no scores before training and no measure of motivation, earlier knowledge, age or drug use; the outcome is answers to unpublished written scenarios, scored against a key partly set by experts who are also programme staff, and staff who knew who was trained could help people fill in the questionnaire (card sc_green_2008: ROBINS-I serious).

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: written scenarios, 2005–2006, people recruited at harm-reduction programmes. As an answer about recognising a real overdose today, fentanyl included, it would be rated lower still, which the statement says; the rating is already at its floor.

imprecision.note: 30 and 32 people, but the differences in opioid recognition and in the naloxone totals are large against their spread (P < 0.001 and P < 0.0001); the difference in naloxone choices for the 9 opioid overdoses alone is less precise (P < 0.05).

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; no protocol or registration.

rate.reasoning: Observational (a non-randomized comparison of trained and untrained people at one time): starts low; risk of bias −1 (see the domain note); inconsistency, indirectness as worded, imprecision and publication bias 0. Very low. Status single study: no other study of how well people recognise overdose scenarios was read. The claim is worded as an association between having been trained and scores on written scenarios; whether training causes better recognition, how people do at real overdoses, which signs they miss and whether training changes deaths or costs are not shown by this design. The paper's printed recognition percentages do not match its means, and its kappa of 1.0 cannot describe individuals; the statement gives the means and says so. Research findings only: the claim names no signs to look for and no steps to take, which belong to the senior author's emergency guidance (METHODS §8).
rate.population: People recruited by staff at six US overdose-training and naloxone-distribution programmes (Chicago; State of New Mexico; San Francisco; Baltimore; New York City, two programmes), October 2005 to July 2006: 62 respondents, 72.6% men, 85.5% currently or formerly using drugs, 22.6% syringe-exchange staff
rate.exposure: Having been trained in overdose recognition and response by the recruiting programme (a median of 8 months before; trainings of about 15 to 120 minutes)
rate.comparator: People at the same programmes not trained by them (32); and an answer key from 11 medical experts combined by latent class analysis
rate.outcome: Number of 16 written overdose scenarios correctly classified (opioid overdose, or non-opioid overdose or not an overdose) and correctly judged as calling or not calling for naloxone; agreement with the experts (kappa)
rate.magnitude: Green et al. (2008), trained (n = 30) against untrained (n = 32), mean (SD): opioid overdoses recognised 7.13 (1.38) against 5.18 (2.55) of 9, t60 = −3.76, P < 0.001; other scenarios 4.63 (1.40) against 4.28 (1.94) of 7, P = 0.42; recognition total 11.77 (1.92) against 9.47 (3.48) of 16, P < 0.005 (73.6% against 59.2%, editors' calculation; printed as 85.2% against 68.3%); naloxone chosen in opioid overdoses 6.93 (1.76) against 5.77 (2.30) of 9, P < 0.05 (not chosen in 2.1 against 3.2); naloxone correctly not chosen 6.60 (0.72) against 5.32 (1.94) of 7, P < 0.001 (chosen where not called for in 0.4 against 1.7); naloxone total 13.53 (1.96) against 11.09 (2.32) of 16 (84.6% against 69.3%), P < 0.0001. 'Not enough information' in 25.6% of the experts' ratings against 16.0% of trained respondents'. Weighted kappa with the experts 0.85 (0.72–0.98) trained, 0.48 (0.18–0.77) untrained; naloxone kappa 1.0 trained, 0.75 (0.44–1.0) untrained (unit of comparison not stated).
rate.short: Not always. On a written test, people trained by overdose programmes spotted about 7 of 9 opioid overdoses. People without that training spotted about 5 of 9.
rate.rate: One small study. Staff picked who took part, nobody was tested before training, and it used written stories, not real overdoses. It doesn't say which stories people got wrong.

risk_of_bias.note: The human evidence is a case series (card sc_siegel_1984: JBI prevalence checklist, high risk): 10 survivors from one clinic, chosen in an unreported way, recalling the occasion about 5 years later in open-ended interviews, with the accounts sorted by the author without stated definitions or a second rater; with no comparison occasions and no comparison group, a count of 7 of 10 cannot estimate any risk. The animal work is described by its author without figures (card sc_siegel_2005: a short narrative review of his own research programme, high risk).

inconsistency.note: No conflicting study was read; the author's own data include 3 of 10 who recalled nothing distinctive, which he reads as overdoses with a non-learned basis.

indirectness.note: The evidence that setting changes the chance of dying is from rats; the human study interviewed survivors only, although its abstract extends the idea to deaths, and its unusual circumstances include changes of injection and of drug combination that the rat experiment did not test; the human laboratory examples concern alcohol and caffeine, not opioids or overdose.

imprecision.note: Ten people (7 of 10: exact 95% CI 35% to 93%, editors' calculation) and no comparison against which a risk could be estimated.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; the 2005 review cites no study that failed to find setting-specific tolerance.

rate.reasoning: The only human evidence on overdose and setting is a case series of 10 survivors' recollections with no comparison (Siegel, 1984): observational, starts low; down two levels for risk of bias, one for indirectness and one for imprecision; very low. The model and the animal findings come from the same author, described without figures in a short narrative review (Siegel, 2005) and in the 1984 paper's introduction; they show why the idea is plausible and are labelled as animal findings, but they are not evidence about people and do not raise the rating. The 1982 rat experiment itself was not read: the PDF saved under its name is a copy of the 1984 paper. Relation: insufficient evidence, because no study of people compared overdose occasions with ordinary ones. Status: single study (one human study; the 2005 review adds no human overdose data and does not cite it).
rate.population: People who use heroin: in the only human study, 10 people formerly dependent on heroin, in methadone maintenance at one clinic in the New York City area, each with a hospital admission for overdose in their records (8 men, 2 women; mean age 28 at interview), interviewed on average 5 years after the overdose; in the animal work the model's author describes, rats and other species
rate.exposure: Taking an opioid in surroundings, company or circumstances not previously linked with taking it (in the human study, anything the person recalled as unusual on the overdose occasion: an unfamiliar place or company, an unusual injection, an unusual drug combination or the absence of a usual one)
rate.comparator: None in the human study (no comparison with the same people's ordinary occasions of use or with people who did not overdose); in the rat experiment, the same final dose given in the environment previously paired with heroin, to rats with the same heroin history
rate.outcome: Overdose (hospital-treated, survivors only) in people; in animals, tolerance and death after a high dose
rate.magnitude: Siegel (1984): 7 of 10 survivors described the circumstances of the overdose occasion as unusual (70%; exact 95% CI 35% to 93%, editors' calculation): 2 injected in places where they had never injected before; 1 used in his own living room, where he had never taken heroin, with a large group at his wedding celebration, and alone overdosed from the shared supply; 2 described unusual injection procedures; 1 took a barbiturate mixture with heroin against his usual practice; 1 injected heroin without the cocaine he usually combined with it, for the first time in over 9 months; 3 of 10 recalled no distinctive feature. Unfamiliar place or company: 3 of 10 (editors' count). No comparison group, no comparison occasions, no test. Rat experiment (Siegel et al., 1982), as described by its author: rats given a high intravenous heroin dose in the environment previously paired with heroin were more likely to survive than rats with the same history given it in a different environment; no survival figures given. Siegel (2005): no sample size or effect size for any study it cites.
rate.short: Maybe. In rats, heroin was more often deadly in a new place. In people, nobody has tested it well. One study asked 10 overdose survivors what was different.
rate.rate: One tiny study of 10 people's memories, with nobody to compare them with, plus rat experiments from the same researcher. Rat findings don't show what happens in people.

risk_of_bias.note: Cases known through press reports and a court case, gathered without a search or criteria (card sc_darke_2017: editorial, high risk); the text describes their causes of death (beyond the UK case), medical histories and other drugs not at all, and the appendix listing them was not read.

indirectness.note: Second-hand through an editorial; custody only, with neglect described in every case, so nothing transfers to withdrawal elsewhere.

imprecision.note: Eleven cases and no denominator: no rate can be estimated.

rate.reasoning: The evidence is reported cases, seen only through an editorial: a claim seen only through reviews starts from the design of the studies they describe (METHODS 6.3), here observational case reports, so it starts low; down for risk of bias (unsystematic cases that cannot be appraised), indirectness (second-hand; custody only) and imprecision (no denominator); very low. Every supporting anchor is the editorial (narrative-review design on its card), so the claim stays at draft and says in its statement that its figures are second-hand (METHODS 6.3). Relation: insufficient evidence on how often withdrawal kills; the statement says only that deaths have been reported, as the editorial describes them. Status: single study (one editorial).
rate.population: People going through opioid withdrawal in custody (jails and prisons in the United Kingdom and the United States), as described in one editorial

rate.rate: Sixteen studies in several countries all found more deaths out of treatment than in it. But nobody chose at random who stayed, and people who leave may differ in other ways, so how much is due to stopping is unknown.

item.statement: Beliefs can shift after a psychedelic retreat and still be shifted 6 months on.
item.why: In one study, belief in things like other worlds rose a little and was still up 6 months on. But only 122 of over 800 people answered every survey, and most already leaned that way.

lines.short: These studies can't say if it's the truth. But beliefs do shift a bit, towards ideas like other worlds and a conscious universe. The shift was still there 6 months later.
lines.but: There was no comparison group, and only 122 of over 800 people answered every survey. Most already leaned that way.
how: People answered questions a week before a psychedelic retreat or ceremony, then 4 weeks and 6 months after. In the 122 who answered all three, belief in things like other worlds rose a little.
First-timers shifted more. In one exploratory analysis, the shift went with feeling in tune with the group, not clearly with how mystical or visual the trip felt.
In a trial in depression, beliefs shifted after psilocybin. They shifted a little after a standard antidepressant too, and the gap was too small to be sure of.

A survey asked 1,606 people whose beliefs had changed to look back, about 8 years on average. 26 in 100 recalled thinking plants could be conscious before, and 61 in 100 after. Superstitions, like black cats bringing bad luck, didn't rise.

item.statement: It's been shown that psilocybin can change your personality.
item.why: Not proven. People rated themselves a little more open after, but the one test against another drug found no difference.

lines.short: Not proven. After psilocybin, people rated themselves about 3 to 5 points more 'open' 1 to 3 months later, on a scale where the average adult scores 50.
lines.but: These were people rating themselves, before and after. The one test against another drug found no difference. Neither study checked how people acted.
how: 52 healthy volunteers, new to psychedelics and mostly religious or spiritual, rated themselves 2.8 points more open 1 to 2 months after their psilocybin session. Their other four traits didn't clearly change.

The rise came from the 30 who had a full mystical experience, and about a third of all the volunteers scored lower afterwards. Over a year later, that group was still about 4 points up, a result right on the edge of chance.
Most of them came from one trial. There, 15 people who got psilocybin first and 15 who got a stimulant first scored no differently on personality 2 months later.

In 19 patients with hard-to-treat depression, openness rose 4.9 points by 3 months, and they rated themselves less anxious and more sociable. The researchers say mood may explain those last two changes.

item.statement: The simple shapes people see on LSD have been sorted into just four types.
item.why: Lattices and honeycombs, cobwebs, tunnels, and spirals. Similar visions also come with flickering light or when falling asleep.

lines.short: Maybe the visual brain's own wiring. A maths model shows how tunnels, spirals, cobwebs and honeycombs could arise there. It wasn't tested in people on a drug.
lines.but: It's only maths: the drug is just a setting for how excitable the brain is. The match was judged by eye against a few drawings.
how: People see simple shapes after LSD or cannabis. They also come with flickering light or when falling asleep. Long ago, these were sorted into four types: lattices and honeycombs, cobwebs, tunnels, and spirals.
The wiring from eye to brain turns a tunnel or a spiral into plain stripes. These run across the brain's first area for sight.
In the model, when that area gets too excitable, stripes and lattices of activity form by themselves, shaped by how its cells connect. Mapped back to what you'd see, they look like all four types.
The wiring data came mostly from cats and monkeys. The best matches needed wider connections than that anatomy shows, and some complex visions don't fit the model.

item.statement: Most men get harder erections on MDMA.
item.why: In one survey of 20 men, 8 said erections got weaker on MDMA and 8 said stronger. They were remembering past experiences, and nobody tested their pills.

lines.short: Desire often goes up, erections can go either way, and orgasm often takes longer. In one survey, 8 of 20 men said erections got weaker on MDMA, and 8 stronger.
lines.but: It's 35 people who chose to talk about it, remembering past experiences. Nobody tested their pills.
how: In Israel, 20 men and 15 women who had used MDMA before sex compared it, from memory, with their usual sex. All 35 said desire went up, and 32 said they were more satisfied.
Of the 20 men, 8 said erections got weaker and 8 stronger. Orgasm took longer for 16 of 20 men and 6 of 15 women, and 3 people couldn't reach it, yet still felt more satisfied.
In Northern Ireland, 98 people were interviewed. A little over half said MDMA was more about closeness than sex. Some men couldn't get an erection; others described strong desire.
Some described one-night stands and regret. Condoms were rare on ecstasy, but also rare without drugs, so the study can't show MDMA made sex riskier.

item.statement: In UK reports, most people with low blood salt after MDMA had drunk a lot of liquid.
item.why: At least 10 of 17 cases reported to a UK poisons service had, and the 2 who died had brain swelling. These reports count only people who got ill, so they can't show how often it happens or whether drinking more changes the risk.

lines.short: Possibly. Low blood salt (sodium) after MDMA has been reported, mostly in young people; of 17 UK cases, at least 10 had drunk a lot of liquid.
lines.but: These only count people who got ill. So they can't show how often it happens, or whether drinking more changes the risk.
how: Over 28 months, 17 people aged 15 to 26 were reported to a UK poisons service. Of the 15 who survived, 10 had seizures, 12 had a normal temperature at hospital, and 13 recovered fully.
The 2 who died, aged 15 and 18, had brain swelling. Both had drunk a lot of water, and drank or were given more after they began to feel ill.
In California poison-centre records, 73 of 188 people who had their blood salt measured had a low level. 4 of those 73 died.

The papers think MDMA makes the body hold on to water. In one study, 8 healthy men given one MDMA capsule had a rise in the water-holding hormone, and their blood salt fell a little, not to a low level. It had no proper comparison, and a study of 32 people found no clear rise in a related marker.

item.statement: In a lab study, MDA brought more visions than MDMA, but less anxiety.
item.why: That's what 12 people on MDA reported, set against MDMA results from other people in earlier studies, so it's a weak comparison.

lines.short: It seemed to last longer, with more visuals and less anxiety: at 6 hours MDA was still clearly felt and MDMA wasn't. That's one small lab study.
lines.but: MDA and MDMA weren't tested on the same people. The MDMA results, from other people in earlier studies, stop at 6 hours.
how: 12 healthy adults who had used MDA, or MDMA and LSD-type drugs, took MDA and a dummy pill in hospital, not told which. Their results were set beside earlier MDMA results from other people.
MDA brought more visions with eyes closed and more 'spiritual' feelings than MDMA, and less anxiety and loss of control. Both made people feel close to others.
Heart rate rose about 20 beats a minute after MDA and 31 after MDMA, though the paper calls them similar. Top blood pressure rose about 30 points with both.
The paper calls MDA well tolerated but gives no side-effect data at all. Why MDMA is more popular wasn't studied.

item.statement: In a lab test, LSD and psilocybin trips felt much alike. The big difference was how long they lasted.
item.why: In 28 people, LSD lasted about 9 to 11 hours and psilocybin 6 to 7. Ratings barely differed, but that's no proof they're the same.

lines.short: Mostly how long it lasts: about 9 to 11 hours for LSD, 6 to 7 for psilocybin, the drug in mushrooms. Otherwise 28 people in a lab rated the trips alike.
lines.but: Finding no difference in 28 people doesn't prove there is none. And most could tell which drug they'd had.
how: 28 healthy adults each had five hospital days, at least 10 days apart. They got a dummy, two amounts of LSD and two of psilocybin, in random order, not told which.
LSD lasted longer at both amounts. It also began a bit sooner, which the authors put down to it being a liquid, not a capsule.
The higher psilocybin amount raised blood pressure and body temperature a little more. LSD raised heart rate more. Both brought complaints like headaches; nobody had a serious problem.
By the study's own figures, people named the right drug in most sessions, which may have shaped their ratings. It used pure psilocybin in capsules, not mushrooms.

item.why: In 24 people, bad-feeling and fear scores weren't clearly lower than on LSD alone, and nobody tested it at a party.

lines.short: Blood pressure and heart rate went higher than on LSD alone, and bad feelings weren't clearly eased. In a lab study of 24 people, top blood pressure was 13 points higher.
lines.but: Healthy people took one amount of each, in a calm hospital room. Nothing serious happened, but 24 people can't show rare dangers.
how: 24 healthy adults each had four hospital days, at least 10 days apart. They got LSD, MDMA, both at once, or a dummy, in random order and without being told which.

With both, top blood pressure averaged 150, against 137 on LSD alone and 148 on MDMA alone; heart rate 100 beats a minute, against 92 and 95. Body temperature was not clearly higher than on LSD alone.
Bad-feeling, fear and complaint scores were not clearly lower than on LSD alone. Nobody had a serious problem. On nausea, the paper contradicts itself.
The two drugs changed each other's blood levels: more LSD stayed in the blood for longer, while MDMA peaked lower and later.

how: 9 healthy men who had taken MDMA before each had four lab sessions, a week apart. They got MDMA, alcohol, both, or neither, with dummy pills and drinks so they didn't know which.

item.statement: By late 2021, about 15 in 100 overdose deaths in the western US showed signs of fake pills.
item.why: That was up from about 5 in 100 in mid-2019. Death records likely miss many fake pills, so the true share may be higher.

lines.short: Yes, in US records to 2021. Overdose deaths with signs of fake pills rose from 2 to about 5 in 100, and to about 15 in 100 in western states.
lines.but: Nobody tested what share of street pills hold fentanyl. These are police and death records, and death records likely miss many fake pills.
how: US police records: of seizures that held fentanyl, pills were 14 in 100 in early 2018 and 29 in 100 in late 2021. The rest were powder. Fentanyl pills seized in three months rose from about 42,000 to about 2.1 million.

Death records from 29 states and Washington, DC: deaths with signs of fake pills went from 2 in 100 in mid-2019 to a high of about 5 in 100 in mid-2021, then stayed near there. In western states, about 5 became about 15 in 100.

In 2021, 55 in 100 of these deaths involved fake oxycodone only, often marked 'M-30', and 17 in 100 fake alprazolam (Xanax) only. Fentanyl or similar drugs were among the recorded causes in 93 in 100.
Neither record shows what the pills held: police data have no pill contents, and death records don't say how many pills were tested. A drug-checking study in Vancouver tested too few pills to say.

lines.short: Not always. On a written test, people trained by overdose programmes spotted about 7 of 9 opioid overdoses. People without that training spotted about 5 of 9.
lines.but: It was a paper test with 62 people that staff picked, not real overdoses. Nobody was tested before training, so training may not be the reason.
how: In 2005 and 2006, 62 people at six US overdose programmes read 16 short stories. Each was based on what someone who injects drugs had called an overdose. Medical experts had decided 9 were opioid overdoses needing naloxone, and 7 were not.
Trained people spotted about 7 of the 9 opioid overdoses, untrained people about 5. Trained people still didn't choose naloxone in about 2 of the 9; untrained people missed about 3.
Both groups got only about 4 or 5 of the other 7 stories right. Even the experts said there wasn't enough information in about a quarter of their answers.
The paper doesn't say which stories people got wrong. So it can't show which signs get missed, or whether people can tell a heavy nod from an overdose.

item.statement: Pills sold as ecstasy have nearly always held MDMA.
item.why: In European tests in 2009, as few as 19 in 100 pills held MDMA in one country. These were pills people chose to bring in.

lines.short: Often, but not always. In European pill tests in 2009, 19 to 64 in 100 pills held MDMA, depending on the country. By 2013 most did, and held more of it.
lines.but: These were pills people chose to bring in, and the newest tests are from 2013. Pills today may be different.
how: A 2004 review of pill tests found MDMA in 90 to 98 in 100 ecstasy pills from the 1980s to the early 1990s, 50 to 80 in 100 in the mid-1990s, and nearly all by the early 2000s. Others held related drugs, other things such as ketamine or caffeine, or nothing active.

Drug-checking services in five European countries tested pills people brought in, from 2008 to 2013. Pills holding MDMA dropped in 2009, to about 19 in 100 in Austria and 64 in 100 in the Netherlands, then mostly recovered. Newer drugs such as mCPP or PMMA turned up in some ecstasy.

The MDMA in a pill ranged from none to about 150 mg in older tests. Where measured, the average rose from about 61 to 74 mg in 2009 to about 103 to 114 mg in 2013: nearly double in the Netherlands, less elsewhere. These are lab measurements, not amounts to take.

Some people feel little from a pill, and some then take more. A weaker pill, or one with no MDMA, is one possible reason; in an Australian survey, people thought about 1 pill in 4 or 5 was a dud. Neither source looked at other reasons, such as tolerance, or at what happens when people then take more.

item.statement: People on methadone become fully tolerant to its effect on breathing.
item.why: One review describes two studies of people on methadone: their tolerance to its effect on breathing was not complete.

lines.short: Because tolerance may drop during a break, reviews say. In one study, 3 people died of an overdose after a hospital detox. All 3 had stayed for the whole programme.
lines.but: Nobody measured anyone's tolerance. And it's 3 deaths in one small study.
how: 137 people were followed for a year after a 28-day hospital detox in London. All 3 overdose deaths came within 4 months, among the 37 who finished both the detox and the programme. None of the 100 who left earlier died that way.

The researchers read this as lost tolerance but never measured it. The people who died also differed in other ways: 4 of the 5 who died from any cause had lived alone, against 16 in 100 of the others.
Two reviews offer the same idea but give no numbers: not how long a break must be, how fast tolerance falls, or how much the risk rises. The main study behind them looked at hair samples.
One review describes two studies of people on methadone. Their tolerance to its effect on breathing was not complete.
