item.why: The opposite: all 3 overdose deaths came among the 37 who finished it, and none among the 100 who left earlier. The researchers suspect lost tolerance, but nobody measured it.

item.statement: In rats, heroin was more often deadly in a new place than in the usual one.
item.why: In one researcher's rat studies, yes. In people, it has only been looked at in 10 overdose survivors' memories, with nobody to compare them with.

lines.short: Maybe. In rats, heroin was more often deadly in a new place. In people, nobody has tested it well. One study asked 10 overdose survivors what was different.
lines.but: That's 10 people's memories, about 5 years later, with nobody to compare them with. Only 3 of them recalled a new place or crowd.
how: The idea: the place, the people and the ritual that come with a drug start to trigger the body's push-back against it. That push-back is part of tolerance, so it may be weaker somewhere new.
In rat studies from the same researcher, tolerance was weaker in a new place, and a large dose of heroin was more often deadly there. Rats aren't people.
Of 10 overdose survivors, 7 recalled something unusual that day: 3 a new place or crowd, 2 a different way of injecting, 2 a different mix of drugs. The other 3 recalled nothing unusual.
Nobody counted how often people use somewhere new without an overdose. The review suggests a treatment based on the idea, but cites no test of it.

item.statement: Death rates were about the same in and out of methadone treatment.
item.why: In 16 groups of people on methadone, about 11 in 1,000 died each year in treatment, against about 36 out of it. People who leave differ in other ways, so this can't show cause.

lines.short: The weeks after leaving were the riskiest. In 5 studies, deaths in the first 4 weeks off methadone ran at about 32 a year per 1,000 people, against 6 in steady treatment.
lines.but: These studies counted everyone who left, for any reason. People who leave differ in other ways, so the studies can't show that stopping itself caused the deaths.
how: In 16 groups of people on methadone, about 11 in 1,000 died each year in treatment, against about 36 out of it. Every group had more deaths out of treatment.
In the biggest recent groups the gap was smaller: about 6 or 7 deaths a year per 1,000 people in treatment, against 12 to 18 out of it.
Deaths in the first 4 weeks off methadone ran at about 32 a year per 1,000 people, against about 14 later on. The first month on methadone looked riskier too, but that could be chance.
Deaths counted as overdoses didn't clearly rise after leaving, in the 3 groups that split them by time. Buprenorphine had just three groups, mostly one Australian study.

item.statement: You can't die from opioid withdrawal.
item.why: Deaths have been reported, all in jail, linked to vomiting and diarrhoea that dried people out and went untreated. How often it happens is unknown: the list comes from one editorial.

lines.short: It has happened, but nobody knows how often. One editorial lists 11 deaths, all in jail. It links them to vomiting and diarrhoea that dried people out and went untreated.
lines.but: It's one editorial's list, built from news reports and a court case. With no count of how many people went through withdrawal, there's no rate.
how: The authors' idea: vomiting and diarrhoea that don't stop, left untreated, dry the body out. Blood sodium rises, and the heart can fail.
The cases: a woman in custody in the UK in 1998, and 10 people in US jails reported in the press from 2013 to 2016, aged 18 to 49.
The authors say each death came slowly, with time to treat it, and call the deaths neglect or a lack of medical care.
They say such deaths are rising but give no counts over time. Nothing here covers withdrawal outside custody.

lines.statement: In adults who chose to attend a ceremony, retreat or other guided session with a classic psychedelic and signed up for online surveys (mostly from Western countries, highly educated, and already leaning towards non-physicalist views beforehand), attending, compared with their own answers about a week before, is associated with modestly stronger agreement with non-physicalist statements 4 weeks and 6 months later; in one randomized trial in depression the shift after psilocybin therapy exceeded the shift after escitalopram only on a one-tailed test; and none of the studies tests whether the beliefs are true. On a questionnaire written for the study, whose main factor groups belief in other realms that can be visited, a unifying principle beyond scientific explanation, panpsychism (mind as a quality of all things), dualism and idealism against materialism and naturalism (Timmermann et al., 2021), the 122 respondents with answers at all three time points (819 in the baseline table and 866 said to have answered at some time point, so about 85 in 100 are missing from these analyses and were not compared with those who stayed) shifted by d = 0.33 at 4 weeks and d = 0.46 at 6 months, and the 53 taking a psychedelic for the first time by d = 0.53 and 0.73; belief in fatalistic determinism rose at 4 weeks (d = 0.25) but not at 6 months. Positions moved both ways: of respondents classed as 'hard materialists' at baseline, 24.4% still held that position at 4 weeks and 22.2% at 6 months, most of the others moving to a mixed position or to dualism, while 17.6% and 15.2% of respondents with mixed positions moved to materialism; of those neutral on panpsychism, 57.3% and 54.5% became 'believers' (group sizes not printed, and the samples behind these tables not stated). In an exploratory path model, feeling emotionally in tune with the group during the session predicted the 4-week score (standardized beta 0.22), while mystical-type and visual-effect scores were dropped as not significant. In the same team's double-blind trial in 59 adults with major depression, a 5-item version of the questionnaire shifted after psilocybin therapy (two 25 mg doses and 6 weeks of daily placebo, study condition; d = 0.45) and less after 6 weeks of daily escitalopram given with two 1 mg doses of psilocybin (d = 0.2, p = 0.33, which the authors call no change); the difference between the arms had p = 0.041 one-tailed, about 0.08 two-sided (editors' calculation). In a retrospective online survey by another team, of 1,606 adults recruited because they attributed a change in their beliefs to a psychedelic experience, each rating 'before', 'after' and 'now' for their most belief-changing experience in one sitting a mean of 8.2 years after it, the share agreeing that plants can be conscious was 26% before against 61% after, fungi 21% against 56%, insects 33% against 57%, rocks 8% against 26% and the universe 34% against 80%, with 'now' close to 'after'; superstitions (black cats bringing bad luck: 8%, 4% and 3%) and belief in free will (74%, 74% and 73%) did not change meaningfully, and people who remembered a more mystical experience reported larger changes (Nayak & Griffiths, 2022). The cohort cannot separate the drug from the ceremony's group, ritual, teaching and expectations, or show that those who stopped answering changed like those who stayed, and its authors say that views held by co-attendees and by the trial's staff may have passed to participants; the survey, recruited on belief change and relying on memory over years, cannot show how often or how much beliefs change. On truth, the first team writes that judging the value of the positions is beyond its work and that it would be hasty to read its results as favouring them, and the second that persistent beliefs after compelling experiences neither support nor undermine their validity. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated by the same team.
lines.population: Adults who planned to attend a retreat, ceremony or other guided experience with a classic psychedelic and signed up at a study website after online advertisements (819 in the baseline table: mean age 44.4; 55.6% men; 43.8% from the United States and 19.5% from the United Kingdom; 90.7% White; 54.1% with a master's, doctoral or professional degree, editors' sum), of whom 122 answered the belief questions at baseline, 4 weeks and 6 months; 59 adults with major depression (30 and 29) in a randomized trial by the same team; and 1,606 adults recruited online by another team because they attributed a change in their beliefs to a psychedelic experience (mean age 35.1; 67% men; 89% White; 69% from the United States).
lines.exposure: Attending a ceremony or retreat with a classic psychedelic (psilocybin mushrooms or truffles, ayahuasca, DMT, San Pedro, LSD or 1P-LSD), the substance, amount and setting chosen by the respondents and not reported; in the trial, psilocybin therapy: 25 mg on two dosing days and 6 weeks of daily placebo (study condition); in the survey, a past experience with psilocybin mushrooms (49%), LSD (33%), ayahuasca (7%), N,N-DMT (6%), 5-MeO-DMT (3%) or mescaline-containing cacti (2%), chosen by each respondent as the one that most changed their beliefs.
lines.comparator: Each respondent's own answers about a week before the ceremony (no comparison group); in the trial, randomized daily escitalopram for 6 weeks with two 1 mg doses of psilocybin; in the survey, respondents' remembered 'before' beliefs, rated in the same sitting as 'after' and 'now'.
lines.outcome: Agreement with non-physicalist statements: a 9-item factor (Cronbach's alpha 0.86) of a 13-item Metaphysical Beliefs Questionnaire written for the study, and 5 of its items in the trial; fatalistic determinism (FAD-Plus items); changes in the position most strongly endorsed; in the survey, the share agreeing that ten kinds of entity can be conscious, five superstition items and one free-will item. Whether any belief is true was not assessed.
lines.magnitude: Timmermann et al. (2021), cohort, 122 with paired data: non-physicalist factor at 4 weeks t(121) = 3.66, Bonferroni p = 0.001, d = 0.33; at 6 months t(121) = 5.07, p < 0.0001, d = 0.46 (the printed 95% CIs [0.12, 0.39] and [0.22, 0.50] cannot be intervals of d; editors' approximate 95% intervals for d, SE = √(1/n + d²/2n), 0.15 to 0.51 and 0.27 to 0.65); first-timers (53): d = 0.53 and 0.73; fatalistic determinism d = 0.25 at 4 weeks (p = 0.012), not at 6 months. Conversion (Figure 2; group sizes not printed): 'hard materialists' remaining 24.4% (4 weeks) and 22.2% (6 months); dualists remaining 55.5% and 65.2%; none/mixed to materialism 17.6% and 15.2%; panpsychism neutral to believer 57.3% and 54.5%, sceptic to believer 22.6% and 37.8%. Lifetime psychedelic use and baseline factor score: Spearman r = 0.223 (cross-sectional). Path model: emotional synchrony to the 4-week score, beta 0.22. Trial (psilocybin therapy 30, escitalopram 29; 5 items): interaction F(56) = 3.13, p = 0.041 one-tailed (editors' calculation: two-sided p = 0.082); psilocybin Z = 2.28, p = 0.02, d = 0.45; escitalopram Z = 0.24, p = 0.33, d = 0.2 (Z = 0.24 gives a one-tailed p of about 0.41, editors' calculation). Nayak & Griffiths (2022), 1,606, % agreeing before, after and now: plants 26, 61, 64; fungi 21, 56, 62; insects 33, 57, 60; inanimate natural objects 8, 26, 29; inanimate man-made objects 3, 15, 17; the universe 34, 80, 82; self 80, 97, 98; no meaningful change for superstitions (black cats 8, 4, 3; Loch Ness monster 10, 10, 10) or free will (74, 74, 73).
lines.reasoning: Observational evidence (a prospective cohort without a comparison group and a retrospective survey) starts low; rated down two levels for risk of bias, which is below the floor: very low. Rated as worded: an association between attending a psychedelic ceremony and modest shifts in stated beliefs among people who kept answering; not that psychedelics cause the shift, that it is specific to psychedelics (escitalopram also moved, d = 0.2, and the difference between the arms was significant only one-tailed), or that it lasts beyond 6 months. The trial is randomized and would start high on its own, but as the only comparison between treatments it rests on 59 patients, a 5-item version and a one-tailed p of 0.041 (about 0.08 two-sided), so it qualifies the claim rather than raising it. Status replicated by the same team: the cohort and the trial are one group's two samples, reported in one paper; the survey from another group agrees in direction but recruited people because their beliefs had changed and relied on recall, so it is not counted as an independent test. Whether the beliefs are true is outside what any of these designs can address, as both teams say.

lines.q: Do trips show you the truth, or just change your beliefs?
lines.short: These studies can't say if it's the truth. But beliefs do shift a bit, towards ideas like other worlds and a conscious universe. The shift was still there 6 months later.
lines.but: There was no comparison group, and only 122 of over 800 people answered every survey. Most already leaned that way.
how: People answered questions a week before a psychedelic retreat or ceremony, then 4 weeks and 6 months after. In the 122 who answered all three, belief in things like other worlds rose a little.
First-timers shifted more. In one exploratory analysis, the shift went with feeling in tune with the group, not clearly with how mystical or visual the trip felt.
In a trial in depression, beliefs shifted after psilocybin. They shifted a little after a standard antidepressant too, and the gap was too small to be sure of.

A survey asked 1,606 people whose beliefs had changed to look back, about 8 years on average. 26 in 100 recalled thinking plants could be conscious before, and 61 in 100 after. Superstitions, like black cats bringing bad luck, didn't rise.

lines.statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether psilocybin changes personality. In two small studies with no comparison group for the change, self-rated Openness to experience on the NEO Personality Inventory-Revised (T scores: population mean 50, SD 10) was a few points higher 1 to 3 months after psilocybin with preparation and support than each person's own score before; the one randomized comparison of personality in these trials found no difference, no paper checked a change against behaviour, and the two papers disagree on whether the change followed the experience. In 52 healthy, hallucinogen-naive, unpaid volunteers pooled from two double-blind trials at Johns Hopkins (mean age 46; 54% with postgraduate degrees; 90% regularly taking part in religious or spiritual activities; screening Openness 65.4 and 62.7), Openness was 2.8 T points higher 1 to 2 months after the high-dose session (psilocybin 30 mg/70 kg, study condition; F(1, 51) = 5.47, p = 0.023), Neuroticism, Extroversion, Agreeableness and Conscientiousness did not change detectably, and in the 30 whose first session was placebo, methylphenidate or a low psilocybin dose Openness did not change after that session (p = 0.48), though the two changes were never compared with each other (MacLean et al., 2011). The rise was in the 30 who met the criterion for a 'complete mystical experience' (+5.7, p = 0.002), not in the other 22 (−1.2), and it correlated with the session's mystical score (r = 0.42); individual changes ranged from about −12 to +36 T points, about 17 of the 51 visible points in the paper's figure lie below zero (about a third of the volunteers scored lower; editors' reading), and without the three largest rises the other 49 would average about +1.3 (editors' approximate calculation, (2.8 × 52 − 84) / 49). At a mean of 16 months the complete-mystical group was 4.2 points above its screening score at p = 0.050 (0.0503 by the editors' calculation) and the others 0.3 below; the change for all participants together was not reported. In the earlier trial that supplied 35 of these volunteers, the randomized comparison of 15 people given psilocybin first with 15 given methylphenidate first found no difference in any personality factor 2 months later (no values printed; Griffiths et al., 2006, as its checked study card reports), a result MacLean et al. do not mention. In 19 adults with treatment-resistant depression given psilocybin 10 mg and then 25 mg a week later with psychological support in an open-label study in London (Erritzoe et al., 2018; its authors include MacLean et al.'s first author), Neuroticism fell from T 76.6 to 70.9 (p = 0.002), Extraversion rose from 31.1 to 37.6 (p < 0.001) and Openness from 52.7 to 57.6 (p = 0.012) at 3 months, Conscientiousness rose at trend level (p = 0.086) and Agreeableness did not change; Neuroticism, Extraversion and Conscientiousness moved from far outside the norms towards them, and the authors say it is hard to infer that the changes, particularly in Neuroticism and Extraversion, are traits rather than states. The Openness rise did not differ between the 7 patients whose depression responded and the 12 whose did not, and no 'peak experience' score related to it, whereas insightfulness during the session went with the Neuroticism and Extraversion changes in uncorrected, exploratory correlations (r = −0.47 and 0.54). All scores are self-ratings by people who knew, or could probably tell, that they had taken psilocybin, in volunteers drawn to a psilocybin study or to a psychedelic treatment; in the 2006 trial, three people close to each volunteer rated a small positive change in behaviour and attitudes after psilocybin (Griffiths et al., 2006, as its card reports), but no paper read related such ratings, or any behaviour, to the personality scores. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
lines.population: 52 healthy, hallucinogen-naive, unpaid volunteers recruited by community flyers for a study of states of consciousness brought about by psilocybin (35 from a 2006 trial and 17 from a 2011 trial at Johns Hopkins; mean age 46; 22 men and 30 women, editors' sum; 54% with postgraduate degrees; 90% regularly taking part in religious services, discussion groups, prayer or meditation; screening Openness T 65.4 and 62.7); in the 2006 trial, 30 volunteers randomized to drug order (15 per order); and 19 analysed of 20 adults with moderate to severe treatment-resistant unipolar depression in an open-label study in London (6 women, 13 men; mean age 44.7; five had tried a psychedelic before).
lines.exposure: Psilocybin by mouth with preparation and support, as study conditions only: one session at 30 mg/70 kg (in the 2011 trial within four ascending or descending doses with a placebo session), lying down with an eye mask and music, after at least 8 hours of meetings with the session monitors; in the open-label study, 10 mg and then 25 mg a week later, eyes closed with music and two therapists, with integration visits afterwards.
lines.comparator: Each person's own personality scores before (screening or baseline), with no concurrent comparison of change in either main study; within the healthy volunteers, people with and without a 'complete mystical experience' (not randomized) and, separately, change after a first session of placebo, methylphenidate or psilocybin 5 mg/70 kg; in the 2006 trial, people given psilocybin first against people given methylphenidate first (randomized; no values printed).
lines.outcome: Self-rated personality on the NEO Personality Inventory-Revised (240 items; five domains of six facets; T scores from combined-sex norms), 1 to 2 months after the session and about 14 months after the last session (a mean of 16 months after the high-dose session) in the healthy volunteers, and 3 months after in the patients; no behavioural measure and no ratings of personality by others.
lines.magnitude: MacLean et al. (2011), 52 volunteers, screening to 1–2 months: Openness +2.8 T points, F(1, 51) = 5.47, p = 0.023, partial eta squared 0.10 (editors' calculation: within-person standardized change about 0.32, √(5.47/52)); Neuroticism −0.5 (p = 0.62), Extroversion +0.8 (p = 0.38), Agreeableness +1.7 (F = 2.31, printed p = 0.16; 0.13 by the editors' calculation), Conscientiousness −0.9 (p = 0.28). After a first session without high-dose psilocybin (30): F(1, 29) = 0.52, p = 0.48. Complete mystical experience (30) against not (22): F(1, 50) = 9.32, p = 0.004; +5.7 (t(29) = 3.44, p = 0.002) against −1.2 (t(21) = 0.87, p = 0.39). Mystical score and Openness change r = 0.42, p = 0.002 (editors' 95% CI about 0.17 to 0.62, Fisher z). Follow-up (mean 16 months): complete group +4.2, F(1, 29) = 4.17, p = 0.050 (0.0503 by the editors' calculation); others (21) −0.3, p = 0.86; all participants not reported. Figure 1 (editors' reading): changes from about −12 to +36, about 17 of 51 visible points below zero; about +1.3 without the three largest (editors' approximate calculation). Griffiths et al. (2006, card): no personality factor differed between order groups (15 and 15) at 2 months; no values. Erritzoe et al. (2018), 19 patients, baseline to 3 months (T scores): Neuroticism 76.6 to 70.9 (−5.7, p = 0.002), Extraversion 31.1 to 37.6 (+6.5, p < 0.001), Openness 52.7 to 57.6 (+4.9, p = 0.012), Agreeableness 46.8 to 46.7 (p = 0.953), Conscientiousness 29.9 to 33.1 (+3.2, p = 0.086); printed d −0.571, 0.716, 0.437, −0.006 and 0.273, from a formula whose denominator is not divided by 2 (about 0.71 times the usual average-SD d; editors' calculation); Openness change in responders (7) against non-responders (12) 11 ± 21 against 7 ± 6, p = 0.623 (units not stated); insightfulness with Neuroticism change r = −0.47 (p = 0.043) and with Extraversion change r = 0.54 (p = 0.017), uncorrected; no peak-experience score related to the Openness change.
lines.reasoning: The personality estimates are before-and-after changes within the same people, not comparisons between randomized conditions, so they are rated as observational and start low; rated down two levels for risk of bias and one each for inconsistency, indirectness and imprecision, which is below the floor: very low. Worded as insufficient evidence on whether psilocybin changes personality: that self-rated Openness was a few points higher after than before in these two samples is reported in the statement, not rated as an effect of the drug. Counted once: the 2006 trial supplied 35 of MacLean's 52 volunteers, so its null comparison and MacLean's rise come largely from the same people; the patient study is from a London team that includes MacLean's first author, and its Openness rise points the same way under different conditions. Status contested: the before-and-after rises point one way, and the one randomized comparison, the subgroup on which the lasting change rests and the two papers' disagreement about the experience point the other; the debate box sets out both sides. Neither paper checked a change against behaviour.

lines.short: Not proven. After psilocybin, people rated themselves about 3 to 5 points more 'open' 1 to 3 months later, on a scale where the average adult scores 50.
lines.but: These were people rating themselves, before and after. The one test against another drug found no difference. Neither study checked how people acted.
how: 52 healthy volunteers, new to psychedelics and mostly religious or spiritual, rated themselves 2.8 points more open 1 to 2 months after their psilocybin session. Their other four traits didn't clearly change.

The rise came from the 30 who had a full mystical experience, and about a third of all the volunteers scored lower afterwards. Over a year later, that group was still about 4 points up, a result right on the edge of chance.
Most of them came from one trial. There, 15 people who got psilocybin first and 15 who got a stimulant first scored no differently on personality 2 months later.

In 19 patients with hard-to-treat depression, openness rose 4.9 points by 3 months, and they rated themselves less anxious and more sociable. The researchers say mood may explain those last two changes.

lines.statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether the simple geometric visions seen on psychedelics come from spontaneous patterns of activity in the primary visual cortex (V1): a mathematical model proposes that they do, the paper tests it against no measurement in people on a drug (Bressloff et al., 2001), and no such test has been read for this answer. The model starts from Klüver's sorting of reported geometric hallucinations into four classes of 'form constants': gratings, lattices, fretworks, filigrees, honeycombs and chequer-boards; cobwebs; tunnels, funnels, alleys, cones and vessels; and spirals. The paper says such images are seen after flickering light, certain anaesthetics, deep pressure on the eyeballs, on waking or falling asleep, and shortly after drugs such as LSD and marijuana, and, citing earlier reports, that they are also seen by blind people and in sealed dark rooms and keep their positions relative to each other as the eyes move, so that they arise in the brain rather than the eyes. The model rests on the map from retina to V1, which away from the centre of gaze works like a complex logarithm, so that circles in the visual field fall on V1 as vertical lines, rays as horizontal lines and logarithmic spirals as oblique lines, making tunnels, funnels and spirals simple stripes of activity across V1; and on the wiring of V1, with cells tuned to the orientation of edges, connections within each local patch, and long lateral connections that link patches of the same orientation preference along the axis of that preference, measured mainly in cats, macaques, owl monkeys and tree shrews and scaled to human V1 (hypercolumns about 1.33 to 2 mm apart, about 1,300 per hemisphere); it extends an earlier model by the corresponding author and a colleague (Ermentrout & Cowan, 1979), which had no orientation tuning and could not produce lattice tunnels, honeycombs, some chequer-boards or cobwebs. When the model's resting state is made unstable, by raising excitability or lowering inhibition, which the authors describe as thought to be one possible effect of hallucinogens, a limited set of repeating patterns can arise: with weak inhibition between neighbouring orientation patches, light-and-dark patterns that map back to tunnels, funnels and spirals, and with strong inhibition, lattices of oriented edges that map back to honeycombs, chequer-boards and cobwebs (elsewhere the paper lists chequer-boards among the light-and-dark patterns instead). Its limits: the drug appears only as an abstract excitability setting, with no receptor, drug or dose, and the same mechanism is offered for flickering light; the match with hallucinations was judged by eye against a few drawings redrawn from secondary sources; the contour-forming patterns that match seen form constants needed lateral connections spreading more than 45 degrees from the orientation axis, wider than the anatomy that motivated the model, whose strict form gave patterns without continuous contours; the expected size of the patterns rests on an unsourced figure of 30 to 40 repetitions around the visual field (2.4 to 3.2 mm in V1); and some reported images, including a complex image after LSD, cannot be explained by the simple model, the authors say. The paper offers predictions, such as orientation changes detectable by optical imaging near the horizontal meridian, that it did not test. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
lines.population: No participants: a mathematical model of human primary visual cortex (V1), built from anatomical and physiological findings in cats, macaques, owl monkeys and tree shrews (partly unpublished, cited as personal communications) and from estimates of human V1 size and hypercolumn spacing, and compared with published drawings and descriptions of geometric hallucinations.
lines.exposure: In the model, a rise in network excitability (stronger global coupling, or a steeper neural response through a steady input) or a fall in local inhibition, which the authors describe as one possible effect of hallucinogens and also apply to flickering light; no drug, receptor or dose is modelled.
lines.comparator: The model's uniform resting state, and the earlier Ermentrout–Cowan model without orientation tuning; for the hallucinations, comparison by eye with a few drawings.
lines.outcome: Which repeating (doubly periodic) patterns of V1 activity can emerge when the resting state becomes unstable, which of them are stable, and what they would look like in the visual field after an inverse retinocortical map; resemblance to Klüver's four classes of form constants, judged by eye.
lines.magnitude: No statistical estimates. Retinocortical map constants w0 = 0.087 and epsilon = 0.051 (estimated from Drasdo, 1977); orientation preference repeating about every 300 µm in cat V1 and 0.5 mm in macaque V1; 20% of lateral connections ending on inhibitory cells; human V1 about 3,500 mm² per hemisphere, hypercolumn spacing about 1.33–2 mm, about 1,300 hypercolumns; critical wavelength given as about 2.66 mm (2π × 0.400 / qc at qc = 1 gives 2.51 mm, editors' calculation); 30–40 repetitions around the visual field for commonly reported hallucinations (unsourced), corresponding to 2.4–3.2 mm in V1; contour-forming (even) patterns need lateral spread beyond 45 degrees (theta0 > π/4).
lines.reasoning: A theoretical model is not evidence from measurement and starts low; rated down one level for risk of bias (the fit to hallucinations judged by eye against a few redrawn images, unsourced premises, sensitivity to the assumed connectivity) and one for indirectness (no human or drug data; the drug as an abstract parameter; animal anatomy), which is below the floor: very low. Worded as insufficient evidence on whether psychedelic geometric visuals arise this way: what the model proposes, what it rests on and what it predicts are reported as such, not rated as findings about the brain. Status single study: one modelling paper; it extends the corresponding author's earlier model (Ermentrout & Cowan, 1979), which is not counted as independent support, and no empirical test of its predictions has been read.

lines.q: Why do psychedelic visuals look like tunnels, spirals and honeycombs?
lines.short: Maybe the visual brain's own wiring. A maths model shows how tunnels, spirals, cobwebs and honeycombs could arise there. It wasn't tested in people on a drug.
lines.but: It's only maths: the drug is just a setting for how excitable the brain is. The match was judged by eye against a few drawings.
how: People see simple shapes after LSD or cannabis. They also come with flickering light or when falling asleep. Long ago, these were sorted into four types: lattices and honeycombs, cobwebs, tunnels, and spirals.
The wiring from eye to brain turns a tunnel or a spiral into plain stripes. These run across the brain's first area for sight.
In the model, when that area gets too excitable, stripes and lattices of activity form by themselves, shaped by how its cells connect. Mapped back to what you'd see, they look like all four types.
The wiring data came mostly from cats and monkeys. The best matches needed wider connections than that anatomy shows, and some complex visions don't fit the model.

lines.statement: In 28 healthy, screened adults (14 women, 14 men; mean age 35; half had used a psychedelic before) who each took LSD (100 and 200 µg as labelled, in solution), psilocybin (15 and 30 mg, in capsules of the pure drug, not mushrooms) and a dummy, one per hospital session at least 10 days apart, in random, counterbalanced order under double-blind, double-dummy conditions (study conditions), LSD compared with psilocybin made the effects last longer and raised heart rate more, while the higher psilocybin dose raised blood pressure and body temperature more; ratings of what the experience was like did not differ significantly between the higher psilocybin dose and either LSD dose on almost every scale, which in 28 people does not show that the experiences are the same (Holze et al., 2022). Length: from each person's 'any drug effect' ratings (a modelled curve, counted from and to 10% of the person's own peak), the effects lasted on average 5.6 hours (SD 2.2) after psilocybin 15 mg, 6.5 (2.4) after 30 mg, 9.3 (3.2) after LSD 100 µg and 11 (3.7) after 200 µg (both LSD doses longer than both psilocybin doses, p < 0.001); they began on average 0.4 to 0.6 hours after LSD and 0.8 hours after psilocybin, which the authors put down to LSD being a liquid and psilocybin a capsule, not to the drugs, and they say, without a formal test, that LSD's longer half-life in blood (about 4 hours, against about 2.5 for psilocin, the form psilocybin takes in the body) fully explains the longer duration. Kind: psilocybin 30 mg and either LSD dose did not differ significantly on any visual analogue scale or on any subscale of the main altered-states questionnaire (5D-ASC); LSD 200 µg was rated higher than psilocybin 30 mg only on 'ineffability' (how hard the experience was to put into words), and both LSD doses raised 'emotional excitation' on a mood scale more than psilocybin; the lower psilocybin dose gave lower peak ratings than the higher one on several scales. These are non-significant post hoc tests without equivalence margins, with most of the numbers in an online supplement that was not read, so the abstract's conclusion that the two drugs' effects do not differ beyond duration goes further than the tests can. Body: both drugs raised blood pressure, body temperature and pupil size against the dummy; psilocybin 30 mg raised blood pressure and body temperature significantly more than LSD, and both LSD doses raised heart rate more than both psilocybin doses; on the group's average curves the differences were modest (systolic pressure roughly 139 mmHg after psilocybin 30 mg against 131 to 133 after LSD and 118 to 120 on the dummy over the same hours; temperature about 37.6 to 37.7 °C against 37.3 to 37.4 and about 36.7; heart rate about 76 to 82 beats a minute after LSD against about 72 after psilocybin 30 mg and 62 to 65 on the dummy over the same hours (its own early point, at half an hour, was about 69 to 70); editors' reading of the figure, as the peak values are in the unread supplement). Unwanted effects: total scores on a list of complaints in the first 12 hours rose with all four active conditions against the dummy, and from 12 to 24 hours with the higher dose of each drug; within 48 hours, counted by drug, 4 people had a headache after psilocybin and 3 after LSD, 2 had low mood after each, 2 and 1 had nausea, and there was one migraine (LSD) and one nosebleed (psilocybin), with 9 flashback episodes in 5 people within 72 hours (5 after LSD, 4 after psilocybin; what was counted is not explained) and no severe adverse event. Blinding: the dummy was recognised in 96% of sessions, and although the paper says no clear distinction between LSD and psilocybin could be made, by its own percentages people named the right drug (either dose) in at least 64% of psilocybin 15 mg sessions, 86% of psilocybin 30 mg sessions, 78% of LSD 100 µg sessions and 79% of LSD 200 µg sessions (editors' calculation: correct guesses plus guesses of the other dose of the same drug), so expectation may have shaped the ratings. How strongly people felt each condition varied widely from person to person (ranges in Table 1), and nobody took a second dose, so taking more was not tested. The study did not test which amounts of the two drugs match, and this answer gives none; the authors' figures on matching amounts rest on doses this study did not give. Three printed values for LSD 100 µg are impossible: two means in Table 1 and one in the pharmacokinetics paragraph lie outside their own ranges. The volunteers had little drug experience (at most 10 lifetime uses of illicit drugs other than cannabis) and no personal or family history of major psychiatric illness, and were in a calm hospital room with an investigator; the LSD solution held about 15% less than its label (84.5 µg per 100 µg unit). Certainty: low. Status: single study.
lines.population: 28 healthy, screened adults (14 women, 14 men; mean age 35, range 25 to 52), recruited by word of mouth or from a pool of people interested in psychedelic trials, and paid; 14 had used a psychedelic before and 10 had never used an illicit drug other than cannabis; excluded were a personal or first-degree family history of major psychiatric disorder, interfering medicines and more than 10 lifetime uses of illicit drugs (cannabis excepted); Basel
lines.exposure: Single oral doses of LSD base as a solution, labelled 100 and 200 µg (analysed content 84.5 µg per 100 µg unit), given double-blind and double-dummy in a calm hospital room with one investigator, in random, counterbalanced order with at least 10 days between sessions (study conditions)
lines.comparator: Psilocybin 15 and 30 mg in capsules (analysed 4.61 mg per 5 mg capsule) and placebo, in the same people on other days
lines.outcome: Duration and onset of self-rated effects (modelled from 'any drug effect' ratings); peak self-ratings on visual analogue scales, the 5D-ASC (primary outcome, rated at 24 hours), mystical-experience and mood scales; blood pressure, heart rate, body temperature and pupil size; complaint scores for 0 to 12 and 12 to 24 hours and adverse events within 48 to 72 hours; guesses of which drug was given
lines.magnitude: Holze et al. (2022), 28 people. Table 1 (mean ± SD, range; psilocybin 15 mg, psilocybin 30 mg, LSD 100 µg, LSD 200 µg): effect duration 5.6 ± 2.2 (2.5–10), 6.5 ± 2.4 (3.7–12), 9.3 ± 3.2 (5.7–17) and 11 ± 3.7 (5.4–20) h, F(3,81) = 34.4, p < 0.001, both LSD doses longer than both psilocybin doses (p < 0.001); time to onset 0.8 ± 0.3, 0.8 ± 0.4, 0.6 ± 0.2 and 0.4 ± 0.2 h, F(3,81) = 12.5 (LSD 100 µg different only from psilocybin 30 mg, p < 0.05; LSD 200 µg from both, p < 0.001). Peak subjective effects: psilocybin 30 mg against either LSD dose, no significant difference on any visual analogue scale or 5D-ASC subscale; LSD 200 µg against psilocybin 30 mg different only on MEQ ineffability; both LSD doses higher than psilocybin on AMRS emotional excitation (statistics in unread Supplementary Tables S1–S4). Autonomic (direction and significance from the text; approximate peaks of the group mean curves read from Fig. 3, not the per-person maxima analysed): systolic about 139 (psilocybin 30 mg), 134 (15 mg), 131–133 (LSD) and 118–120 mmHg (placebo); diastolic about 88, 84, 80–81 and 73–74 mmHg; heart rate about 81–82 (LSD 200 µg), 76–77 (LSD 100 µg), 72 (psilocybin 30 mg), 67–68 (15 mg) and 62–65 bpm (placebo); temperature about 37.65 (psilocybin 30 mg), 37.3–37.4 (other active conditions) and 36.7 °C (placebo). Complaints: acute (0–12 h) scores raised by all four active conditions against placebo, subacute (12–24 h) by LSD 200 µg and psilocybin 30 mg (values in unread Supplementary Table S6). Events within 48 h, by drug (psilocybin, LSD): headache 4 and 3; migraine 0 and 1; nosebleed 1 and 0; low mood 2 and 2; nausea 2 and 1; nightmares 1 and 0; restlessness 1 and 1; vivid dreams 0 and 1; insomnia 1 and 0; involuntary leg movements 0 and 1; flashbacks 9 episodes in 5 people within 72 h (4 after psilocybin, 5 after LSD); no severe adverse events. Half-lives (geometric mean, range): LSD 4.3 (2.5–6.0) and 4.0 (2.3–7.1) h; psilocin 2.4 (1.7–3.1) and 2.7 (1.9–3.4) h. Blinding: placebo identified in 96% of sessions; the given condition named correctly in 64%, 57%, 57% and 61% of sessions; the right drug, either dose, in at least 64%, 86%, 78% and 79% (editors' calculation from the printed percentages).
lines.reasoning: Randomized, counterbalanced within-person comparison: starts high (METHODS 6.3). Risk of bias −1 (self-ratings under weak blinding between the two drugs, statistics held in the supplement, impossible printed values) and imprecision −1 (28 people; sameness in kind cannot be shown without equivalence testing) give low. The duration difference on its own (about 9 to 11 hours against 6 to 7, in the same people, with a decisive test and a plausible link to the half-lives) would be rated moderate, held down only by the self-rated outcome; the statement that the experiences were alike in kind would be rated low or lower, and is worded as not shown either way. Status single study: the first within-person comparison, from one laboratory. The authors' dose-equivalence figures rest on doses not given in this study and are not used; no comparison of strength is made.

lines.q: LSD or mushrooms: what's actually different?
lines.short: Mostly how long it lasts: about 9 to 11 hours for LSD, 6 to 7 for psilocybin, the drug in mushrooms. Otherwise 28 people in a lab rated the trips alike.
lines.but: Finding no difference in 28 people doesn't prove there is none. And most could tell which drug they'd had.
how: 28 healthy adults each had five hospital days, at least 10 days apart. They got a dummy, two amounts of LSD and two of psilocybin, in random order, not told which.
LSD lasted longer at both amounts. It also began a bit sooner, which the authors put down to it being a liquid, not a capsule.
The higher psilocybin amount raised blood pressure and body temperature a little more. LSD raised heart rate more. Both brought complaints like headaches; nobody had a serious problem.
By the study's own figures, people named the right drug in most sessions, which may have shaped their ratings. It used pure psilocybin in capsules, not mushrooms.

lines.statement: In 12 healthy volunteers who had used MDA, or both MDMA and a classic psychedelic, before, one dose of MDA by mouth in hospital (1.4 mg/kg, 83 to 128 mg; study condition), compared not with MDMA in the same people but with MDMA data (1.5 mg/kg; study condition) from other volunteers in two earlier studies by the same team, whose results are shown for 6 hours instead of the 8 recorded after MDA (the paper states the 6-hour limit for heart rate and blood pressure), was associated with effects that lasted longer, more visual and 'spiritual' effects, fewer anxious ones and a smaller rise in heart rate (Baggott et al., 2019). Because this comparison is across separate studies and not randomized, and the MDMA volunteers are not described (16 in some analyses, 12 in others), any of these differences may come from who was studied or how long they were watched rather than from the drugs. Length: at 6 hours no MDMA rating was still significantly above its dummy pill, whereas all five general drug-effect ratings still were after MDA (any drug effect 46.4 points above its dummy pill on a 0 to 100 scale, and 41.6 points above MDMA, at that hour); at 8 hours all but the bad-effect rating were still raised after MDA, a time for which the paper shows no MDMA results. Kind: on a 66-item altered-states questionnaire rated at 8 hours for the peak of the experience (12 people per drug), MDA was rated higher than MDMA on complex and elementary visual imagery and on spiritual experience, and only MDA raised 'audio-visual synesthesia' (sounds changing what is seen); MDMA was rated higher than MDA on anxiety, 'dread of ego dissolution' and impaired control and thinking, three scales on which MDA did not differ from its dummy pill; both drugs raised blissful state, 'oceanic boundlessness', visionary changes, insightfulness, a sense of unity, changed meaning of things perceived and feeling out of the body. Against its dummy pill MDA raised ratings of feeling close to others, as MDMA did against its own (the two did not differ significantly), while on a scale of social feelings only MDMA raised warmth toward others ('Affiliation'; no statistic printed). The authors' description of MDA as more inward and emotionally intense, and of MDMA as more outgoing, is their impression, without data. Heart and blood pressure: heart rate rose by 20 (± 3) beats a minute after MDA against 30.6 (± 4.5) after MDMA (p = 0.03), although the abstract and discussion call the rises similar; MDA's highest reading came from 8 hourly measurements and MDMA's from 6, and a longer window can only raise a maximum, so the window does not explain MDA's smaller rise (editors' reasoning); the highest systolic pressure rose by 33 and 31 mmHg and diastolic by 24 and 19 mmHg (difference p = 0.06). Unwanted effects: over the whole session, ratings of a bad drug effect were not significantly above either dummy pill (at 6 hours MDA's was), and ratings of feeling anxious or paranoid showed no significant effect of condition; the abstract calls MDA well tolerated, but the paper reports no adverse events at all, although its methods describe safety monitoring and a check two weeks later. MDA's half-life in blood averaged 10.9 hours (SD 4); the paper compares it with MDMA figures from another team's study, and its abstract and discussion disagree on whether the half-life explains the longer effects. The volunteers were screened, healthy and experienced, few of them women (number not given), in hospital, given one known dose each; MDA and its dummy pill came on consecutive days, with MDA still in the blood on the second day in the half who had the dummy pill second; nobody took a second dose, so taking more was not studied; people with heart disease were excluded, and the authors say the blood-pressure rises could matter for them. The paper did not ask why MDMA is more widely used than MDA. Its authors write, citing other papers, that MDA is often sold as 'ecstasy' in place of MDMA. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
lines.population: 12 healthy, screened adult volunteers with earlier self-reported experience of MDA, or of both MDMA and a classic psychedelic such as LSD, and no drug dependence other than nicotine or caffeine (mean age 27.8, SD 8; few women, number not given), studied during one hospital stay in San Francisco; MDMA comparison data from 12 to 16 other volunteers in two earlier studies by the same team, not described in this paper
lines.exposure: One oral dose of racemic MDA, 1.4 mg/kg (83 to 128 mg), in a capsule after a two-hour fast, given double-blind by researchers in hospital (study conditions)
lines.comparator: Placebo in the same 12 people on the day before or after (half in each order; how the order was set is not stated); for the drug comparison, racemic MDMA 1.5 mg/kg and its placebo given to other volunteers in two earlier studies by the same team (not randomized against MDA; self-ratings and heart rate recorded to 6 hours instead of 8)
lines.outcome: Self-rated drug effects over time (visual analogue scales, to 8 hours after MDA and 6 after MDMA); a 66-item altered-states questionnaire rated at 8 hours for the peak; affect and social-feeling scales before and 2.5 hours after dosing; heart rate and blood pressure hourly; unwanted effects as rated (no adverse-event data reported); MDA's half-life in blood
lines.magnitude: Baggott et al. (2019): MDA n = 12; MDMA comparison n = 16 (visual analogue scales) or 12 (altered-states and affect and social scales). Length: at 6 h no MDMA effect significantly above its placebo; MDA raised all five general drug-effect items at 6 h and all except bad drug effect at 8 h; any drug effect at 6 h 41.6 ± 7 points above MDMA (z = 6.3, p < 0.001) and 46.4 ± 7 above placebo (z = 6.7, p < 0.001); at 8 h 35.6 ± 10 above placebo (t = 3.7, p = 0.001); MDMA not recorded beyond 6 h. Altered-states questionnaire (F(3,21), Westfall-corrected pairwise tests, printed in Figure 1): complex imagery 20.6, elementary imagery 13.9, spiritual experience 24.8 (MDA > MDMA; both > placebo); dread of ego dissolution 15.1, impaired control and cognition 11.1, anxiety 5.09 (p = 0.008) (MDMA > MDA; MDMA > placebo; MDA not > placebo); audio-visual synesthesia 8.26 (MDA > placebo only); oceanic boundlessness 35.9, visionary changes 21.3, blissful state 32.4, insightfulness 19.4, changed meaning of percepts 13.1, experience of unity 17.9, disembodiment 10.8 (both > placebo; no difference between the drugs). Closeness to others (area under the curve, mean ± SEM): MDA 168.0 ± 53 against its placebo 11.5 ± 38; MDMA 114.4 ± 44 against its placebo −12.5 ± 16; MDA and MDMA not significantly different (F(3,21) = 5.26, p = 0.0073). Affiliation raised by MDMA only (no statistic printed). Bad drug effect area 47.9 ± 26 (MDA) and 41.4 ± 16 (MDMA), neither significantly above its placebo (F(3,21) = 3.1, p = 0.0487, no significant pairwise difference); anxious F(3,21) = 1.26, p = 0.3116; paranoia F(3,21) = 1.71, p = 0.196. Heart rate rise 20 ± 3 bpm (MDA) against 30.6 ± 4.5 (MDMA), p = 0.03; peak systolic rise 33 ± 2 against 31 ± 3 mmHg; diastolic 24 ± 2 against 19 ± 2 mmHg, p = 0.06 (the ± is not defined in this paragraph); main effects of condition F(3,22) = 17.1 (heart rate), 61.7 (systolic) and 32.4 (diastolic), p < 0.0001. Prolactin rise 16 ± 6 against 29 ± 6 ng/mL (p = 0.07); cortisol 16 ± 1 against 13 ± 2 µg/dL. MDA half-life 10.9 ± 4 h (mean ± SD); the MDMA half-life compared, 8.1 ± 2 h, is from Kolbrich et al. (2008a; 1.6 mg/kg; another team). No adverse-event data reported. The paper's areas under the curve for any drug effect, high, good drug effect and liking are not used here: they mix strength with length, and the recording windows differed.
lines.reasoning: The MDA–MDMA comparison is across separate studies and not randomized, so it is rated as observational and starts low (METHODS 6.3; brief for round pdf-2026-11-14), although MDA against its own placebo is a within-person, placebo-controlled comparison. Risk of bias −1 and imprecision −1 give very low (the scale stops there). MDA's effects against its own placebo (raised self-ratings, closeness, perceptual changes, heart rate and blood pressure, effects still present at 8 hours) would be rated higher on their own, but the claim is about how MDA differs from MDMA and inherits its weakest necessary link, the cross-study comparison. Status single study: one paper, whose MDMA data come from the same team's earlier studies (not read). Doses are given only as study conditions and no strength comparison is made. The abstract's 'well-tolerated' has no adverse-event data behind it, which the statement says.

lines.q: How is MDA different from MDMA?
lines.short: It seemed to last longer, with more visuals and less anxiety: at 6 hours MDA was still clearly felt and MDMA wasn't. That's one small lab study.
lines.but: MDA and MDMA weren't tested on the same people. The MDMA results, from other people in earlier studies, stop at 6 hours.
how: 12 healthy adults who had used MDA, or MDMA and LSD-type drugs, took MDA and a dummy pill in hospital, not told which. Their results were set beside earlier MDMA results from other people.
MDA brought more visions with eyes closed and more 'spiritual' feelings than MDMA, and less anxiety and loss of control. Both made people feel close to others.
Heart rate rose about 20 beats a minute after MDA and 31 after MDMA, though the paper calls them similar. Top blood pressure rose about 30 points with both.
The paper calls MDA well tolerated but gives no side-effect data at all. Why MDMA is more popular wasn't studied.

lines.statement: In two small studies of people who had used ecstasy, both from the 1990s and without a comparison group, people described MDMA as often raising sexual desire or feelings of closeness and sensuality while making erections and orgasm harder for some: in a retrospective survey of 35 people who had used MDMA before sex, all reported more desire and 32 more satisfaction, 16 of 20 men and 6 of 15 women a delayed orgasm, and 8 of 20 men weaker erections while another 8 reported stronger ones; in interviews with 98 people, a slight majority described closeness rather than sexual desire. These are recollections of self-selected people, not measurements, so they cannot show how often any of this happens among people who take MDMA, or that MDMA rather than other drugs, expectations or the people themselves caused it. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated (two independent studies agree on the kinds of experiences, not on how often). In Israel, 20 men aged 22 to 46 and 15 women aged 21 to 48 who had occasionally used MDMA before a sexual encounter, healthy, medication-free and without sexual or major psychiatric disorders, rated sex in the 6 hours after MDMA against their usual sex without it, from -3 (profound decrease) to +3 (profound increase), in a structured interview (9 by telephone); how and when they were recruited is not stated, and what their pills contained was not known (Zemishlany et al., 2001). All 35 reported more desire, 34 of them a moderate or profound increase, and most described sex as more sensual than usual; 32 rated satisfaction moderately or profoundly higher (18 of 20 men, 14 of 15 women). Of the 20 men, 8 rated erections worse (4 of them moderately or profoundly), 8 better and 4 unchanged; 12 of 15 women reported more lubrication and 2 less. Orgasm was delayed for 16 of 20 men and 6 of 15 women, and 1 man and 2 women could not reach orgasm at all on MDMA, while orgasm felt more intense to 17 men and 8 women. All 8 men with weaker erections and all 3 people who could not reach orgasm still rated satisfaction moderately or profoundly higher (editors' tally from the paper's table of every person's ratings). With 20 men, the 95% interval around 8 of 20 runs from about 22 to 61 in 100 (editors' calculation). Ten men and 10 women had sometimes taken cannabis with MDMA; the authors say the ratings referred to MDMA alone and did not differ by cannabis use, but print no data. The paper's summary reports the 40 in 100 men with worse erections but not the 40 in 100 with better ones, and its conclusion that MDMA impairs sexual performance rests mostly on delayed orgasm in people who still rated sex as more satisfying; the authors themselves say that expectations may shape such reports. In Northern Ireland, 98 people who used or had used ecstasy were interviewed in depth in 1997 and 1998 (69 in 100 men; aged 17 to 45; 44 in 100 had used ecstasy on at least 100 occasions), recruited through notices, a club magazine, local agencies, the interviewers' contacts, referral by other respondents and paid recruiters, but not in clubs; the findings are themes illustrated by quotations, with no counts and no description of how the interviews were analysed (McElrath, 2005). A slight majority described ecstasy as more about sensuality and deep emotions than sexual desire; some men who tried to have sex described being unable to get an erection or to ejaculate, which seemed to affect men aged 25 or younger more often; other men and women described strongly heightened desire and very good sex; the author suggests that differences in sexual interest between people may explain the range. Some of those who had sex during ecstasy episodes, more often those aged 18 to 25, described multiple partners, one-night stands with strangers or acquaintances, and regret the next day; condoms were rarely used during ecstasy episodes with intercourse, but few respondents used them when no drugs had been taken either, so the study cannot show that MDMA made sex riskier; respondents' views were mixed on whether ecstasy or alcohol led to more risk, and alcohol and other drugs were often taken in the same episodes. The author says the scene has probably changed since 1997 and 1998. Neither study tested the pills, measured sexual function directly or compared occasions with and without MDMA as they happened; the Israeli sample was chosen for having used MDMA before sex, which may be why everyone there reported more desire while a slight majority of the Northern Irish sample described closeness rather than desire (editors' reading).
lines.population: People who had used ecstasy, in two self-selected samples: 35 in Israel (20 men aged 22 to 46, 15 women aged 21 to 48) who had occasionally used MDMA before sex, healthy, medication-free and without sexual or major psychiatric disorders, recruitment not described; 98 current or former users in Northern Ireland interviewed in 1997 and 1998 (69% men; aged 17 to 45; 16% gay or bisexual), recruited through notices, a magazine, agencies, contacts, referral and paid recruiters
lines.exposure: MDMA as ecstasy tablets or pills taken by people's own choice, content and amount unknown and not tested (self-reported; in Israel, cannabis sometimes taken with MDMA by 20 of the 35; in Northern Ireland, alcohol and other drugs often taken in the same episodes)
lines.comparator: Each person's memory of their usual sex without MDMA (Israel); none in Northern Ireland, where respondents compared experiences in their own words
lines.outcome: Recalled sexual desire, erection or lubrication, delay and intensity of orgasm, and satisfaction, each rated from -3 to +3 against usual function (Israel); themes in interviews on sensuality, desire, sexual performance and sexual risk (Northern Ireland)
lines.magnitude: Zemishlany et al. (2001), Table I (20 men, 15 women; counts by the editors from the per-person ratings, which match the text's percentages): desire up 35 of 35, moderately or profoundly 34; satisfaction moderately or profoundly up 32 of 35 (Wilson 95% interval 78% to 97%, editors' calculation), men 18 of 20, women 14 of 15; erection worse 8 of 20 men (22% to 61%; 4 moderately or profoundly), better 8, unchanged 4; lubrication more 12 of 15 women (55% to 93%), less 2, unchanged 1; orgasm delayed 16 of 20 men (58% to 92%) and 6 of 15 women (20% to 64%); no orgasm on MDMA 1 man and 2 women; orgasm more intense 17 of 20 men and 8 of 15 women, less intense 1 man and 3 women; satisfaction +2 or +3 in all 8 men with weaker erections and all 3 people without orgasm; cannabis sometimes with MDMA 10 men and 10 women; interviewed by telephone 9 (printed 25%; 9 of 35 is 26%, editors' calculation). McElrath (2005): 98 interviewed (106, 8 discarded); themes only, no counts ('a slight majority' described sensuality or deep emotions rather than sexual desire).
lines.reasoning: A descriptive claim, rated as a description of the people sampled (METHODS 6.3): starts low; risk of bias -1 and indirectness -1 give very low, the floor; never upgraded. Status replicated: the Israeli survey and the Northern Irish interviews are independent samples by different teams that agree on the kinds of experiences people describe, not on how often each occurs, which neither can show. Neither study measured sexual function, tested the pills or compared occasions with and without MDMA, so the statement makes no causal claim: what people recalled may reflect the drug, other drugs taken (cannabis for 20 of the 35; alcohol often in Northern Ireland), expectations or the people themselves. The Israeli summary's 'erection impaired in 40%' is given with the other 40% who reported better erections, and the risk accounts are given with the finding that condoms were also rare without drugs. Findings only: nothing here is about choosing or using MDMA for sex.

lines.q: What does MDMA do to sex drive, erections and orgasm?
lines.short: Desire often goes up, erections can go either way, and orgasm often takes longer. In one survey, 8 of 20 men said erections got weaker on MDMA, and 8 stronger.
lines.but: It's 35 people who chose to talk about it, remembering past experiences. Nobody tested their pills.
how: In Israel, 20 men and 15 women who had used MDMA before sex compared it, from memory, with their usual sex. All 35 said desire went up, and 32 said they were more satisfied.
Of the 20 men, 8 said erections got weaker and 8 stronger. Orgasm took longer for 16 of 20 men and 6 of 15 women, and 3 people couldn't reach it, yet still felt more satisfied.
In Northern Ireland, 98 people were interviewed. A little over half said MDMA was more about closeness than sex. Some men couldn't get an erection; others described strong desire.
Some described one-night stands and regret. Condoms were rare on ecstasy, but also rare without drugs, so the study can't show MDMA made sex riskier.

lines.statement: In 9 healthy young men who had taken MDMA before (5 to 100 times; on average 26), MDMA (100 mg) taken with alcohol (0.8 g/kg), compared with each drug alone and with a dummy in the same men, one week apart, in random order under double-blind, double-dummy conditions in a quiet laboratory room (study conditions), was associated with feeling as drunk as with alcohol alone but less sleepy, with test scores that fell about as far at their worst as with alcohol alone, and with a little more MDMA and a little less alcohol in the blood (Hernández-López et al., 2002). Feelings: a sedation score rose with alcohol alone but not with both drugs, where it stayed at the level of MDMA alone, and drowsiness ratings were lower with both drugs than with alcohol alone; ratings of feeling drunk rose with alcohol alone and with both drugs, with no significant difference between the two (at their peak about 58 with both drugs and about 40 with alcohol alone on a 100 mm line, editors' reading of the figure), and the authors conclude that MDMA reversed alcohol's sedation but did not reduce drunkenness; ratings of feeling high and stimulated rose with MDMA and with both drugs. Tests: on a timed symbol-matching test (digit symbol substitution), correct answers at the worst point fell by 9.0 with alcohol alone and by 8.11 with both drugs against the dummy (no significant difference between the two), but with both drugs the fall lasted about 1 hour (1 to 2 hours after the capsule) against 2 to 3 hours with alcohol alone, and over 6 hours it did not differ significantly from the dummy; decision time in a reaction test was slower than with the dummy at its peak only with both drugs, for about half an hour. Blood levels: MDMA peaked 13% higher with alcohol (260.29 against 231.42; p = 0.007), with no change in total exposure, and alcohol peaked 15% lower with MDMA (105.81 against 124.62 mg/dl; p = 0.004) and was 9% lower over 6 hours; the authors call these changes mild and within the range of differences between people. The MDMA levels are printed in mg/dl, which cannot be right for these values: the assay's stated range (25 to 400 ng/ml) points to ng/ml. Heart and body: the paper says cardiovascular, hormone and other physiological measures were taken but are not presented, and cites no paper that reports them, so it says nothing about what the mix does to heart rate or blood pressure (body temperature is not named among the measures); no serious adverse reaction occurred and all 9 finished. No rating of one's own performance was taken (the nearest, a scale of feeling energetic and intellectually efficient, was raised more by both drugs than by alcohol alone), and nobody drove: the authors' suggestion that people may feel they are doing better, or drive recklessly, is untested, and they say driving and field studies are needed. The men were healthy, experienced with MDMA, without past bad reactions to it, all with normal activity of a liver enzyme (CYP2D6) that breaks MDMA down, and given one amount of each drug once; women, people new to MDMA, other amounts, repeated doses, heat, dancing and crowds were not studied. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
lines.population: 9 healthy men aged 19 to 36 (mean 23) who had used MDMA recreationally on 5 to 100 occasions (mean 26) and had been drunk before, without past adverse reactions to MDMA or drug dependence other than nicotine (7 smoked), all extensive CYP2D6 metabolizers; recruited by word of mouth and paid; Barcelona
lines.exposure: MDMA 100 mg (racemic, capsule, fasting) with alcohol 0.8 g/kg as vodka and tonic (350 ml drunk over 15 minutes, starting 30 minutes after the capsule), given double-blind and double-dummy in 10-hour outpatient sessions in a quiet room (study conditions, not advice)
lines.comparator: The same men given MDMA with a placebo drink, a placebo capsule with alcohol, and both placebos, one week apart, in an order set by a balanced 4 × 4 Latin square
lines.outcome: Digit symbol substitution test and simple reaction time (impairment as fewer responses or slower times than with placebo), eye-muscle balance (Maddox wing), self-rated sedation and other effects (ARCI) and 23 visual analogue scales including drunken and drowsiness, over 6 to 10 hours; blood MDMA and alcohol; cardiovascular and other physiological measures collected but not reported
lines.magnitude: Hernández-López et al. (2002), 9 men; ANOVA df 3,24 with Tukey tests (Table 1). Sedation (ARCI-PCAG): area alcohol > placebo (p < 0.05) and > combination (p < 0.01), combination not different from placebo or MDMA; peak alcohol > combination (p < 0.05). Drowsiness: area alcohol > placebo and > combination (p < 0.01); peak alcohol > placebo (p < 0.01) and > combination (p < 0.05). Drunken: area and peak raised by alcohol and by the combination against placebo and MDMA (p < 0.01); alcohol against combination not significant; approximate peak ratings about 58 (combination) and 40 mm (alcohol alone), read from Fig. 3. Digit symbol substitution, mean peak differences against placebo: alcohol −5.89 total and −9.0 correct responses, combination −4.89 and −8.11 (peak p < 0.01 for both; alcohol against combination not significant); 6-h area: alcohol against placebo p < 0.01, combination not significant; impairment against placebo lasted 2–3 h with alcohol (from 1 h to 3–4 h) and 1 h with the combination (1–2 h). Reaction decision time, peak: combination against placebo p < 0.05, the only significant pair; the combination's impairment lasted half an hour (1–1.5 h). Euphoria and stimulation scales were raised by MDMA and the combination against placebo and alcohol (not compared here for strength or length). Blood levels (Table 2, mean ± SD; time to peak as median): MDMA peak 231.42 ± 36.20 alone and 260.29 ± 42.22 with alcohol, p = 0.007 (13% higher, the paper's figure), units printed as mg/dl but the assay range is 25–400 ng/ml, so ng/ml is likely; time to peak 1.5 h in both (p = 0.058); area 2447.85 ± 711.81 against 2345.08 ± 838.35, p = 0.471 (headed AUC0–6h, while the methods give AUC0–24h for MDMA, which was sampled only to 10 h). Alcohol peak 124.62 ± 14.94 alone and 105.81 ± 4.99 mg/dl with MDMA, p = 0.004 (15% lower); 6-h area 409.08 ± 24.28 against 371.74 ± 18.67, p < 0.001 (9% lower); time to peak 1.5 against 2 h (p = 0.014). No serious adverse reactions; all 9 completed. Cardiovascular, endocrine and other physiological measures were collected and not reported.
lines.reasoning: Randomized within-person crossover: starts high (METHODS 6.3). Risk of bias −1 and imprecision −2 give very low. The fall in self-rated sedation with both drugs against alcohol alone, and the changes in blood levels, are significant within-person differences and would be rated higher on their own; the claim's main point, that people felt as drunk and did about as badly on the test at its worst, rests on non-significant comparisons in 9 men. Status single study (the dose-finding pilot and the immune results from the same trial were not read). The claim gives risk facts only.

lines.q: What happens when you mix MDMA with alcohol?
lines.short: Just as drunk, but less sleepy, and about as bad on a test at its worst. Blood MDMA also peaked 13% higher, in a lab study of 9 men.
lines.but: Only 9 men, in a lab. Heart measurements were taken but never reported.
how: 9 healthy men who had taken MDMA before each had four lab sessions, a week apart. They got MDMA, alcohol, both, or neither, with dummy pills and drinks so they didn't know which.
With both, the sleepy feeling from alcohol went away. Feeling drunk didn't: if anything, it was rated a bit higher, though not clearly.
On a timed symbol test, scores at their worst fell about as much as with alcohol alone, but for about 1 hour, not 2 to 3. Only with both was reaction time clearly slower than with the dummy.

Blood MDMA peaked 13% higher and blood alcohol 15% lower; the authors call these small changes. Nobody rated how well they thought they did, though they felt more energetic and efficient than with alcohol alone. Nobody drove.

lines.statement: In 24 healthy, screened adults (12 women, 12 men; mean age 30; at most 20 lifetime uses of psychedelics or MDMA) who each took MDMA (100 mg) and LSD (100 µg) at the same time, compared with each drug alone and with a dummy, one per hospital session at least 10 days apart, in block-randomized, counterbalanced order under double-blind, double-dummy conditions in a calm hospital room (study conditions), the combination raised blood pressure and heart rate more than LSD alone, to about the levels of MDMA alone, but not body temperature, did not significantly lower the unwanted effects people rated on LSD, raised LSD's blood levels, and lowered and delayed MDMA's peak (Straumann et al., 2023). Heart and blood pressure (average of each person's highest value, ± SEM): systolic 150 ± 2.9 mmHg with both drugs against 137 ± 2.7 with LSD alone (p < 0.001), 148 ± 2.9 with MDMA alone (not significantly different) and 124 ± 2.4 with the dummy; diastolic 90 against 85 (p < 0.05), 89 and 77; heart rate 100 ± 3.6 beats a minute against 92 ± 4.5 (p < 0.05), 95 and 77. Temperature: 37.5 ± 0.08 °C with both drugs against 37.4 ± 0.06 with LSD alone (not significantly different), 37.3 with MDMA alone (lower than with both drugs, p < 0.05) and 37.0 with the dummy. Unwanted effects: complaint scores in the first 12 hours were 15 (± 2.2) with both drugs and 15 (± 1.9) with LSD alone (8.6 with MDMA alone, 1.9 with the dummy), and from 12 to 24 hours 5.5 against 3.1 (not significantly different); ratings of a bad drug effect (14 against 18 out of 100) and of fear (8.2 against 13) did not differ significantly from LSD alone; headache, lack of energy, loss of appetite and dry mouth were reported about as often with either drug or both; no severe adverse event occurred. On nausea the paper contradicts itself: its results say nausea on the complaint list was more frequent with MDMA than with LSD, its table shows nausea ratings lower with MDMA (7.9 out of 100) than with LSD (25) or both drugs (21), and its discussion says nausea was about as frequent with both drugs as with either alone; the item counts are in a supplement that was not read. Late in the LSD response the authors note trend-level, non-significant signs of lower well-being and more depressed mood with both drugs in some people. Blood levels: with MDMA, LSD's peak was 2.1 against 1.9 ng/mL (p < 0.05), its half-life 5.2 against 3.9 hours (p < 0.001) and its total exposure 19 against 14 ng·h/mL (p < 0.01; about a third more, editors' calculation); with LSD, MDMA's peak was 208 against 233 ng/mL (p < 0.001; about a tenth lower, editors' calculation) and came later, at 3.5 against 2.8 hours (p < 0.01), with total exposure unchanged; the paper's text and abstract mention only the change in LSD's levels. The authors attribute the higher LSD levels to MDMA blocking an enzyme that breaks down drugs (CYP2D6), which they inferred from other studies and did not measure. Their statement that they found no sign of greater serotonin toxicity rests on 24 healthy people given one pair of doses together in a calm room, which cannot show rare or setting-dependent harms; other doses, other timing, repeated doses, heat, dancing, alcohol or other drugs, and people with heart or psychiatric conditions or on interacting medicines were not studied. Certainty: low. Status: single study.
lines.population: 24 healthy, screened adults (12 women, 12 men; mean age 30, range 25 to 54), recruited by word of mouth or from a pool of people interested in psychedelic trials, and paid; 12 had used a psychedelic and 9 MDMA before (1 to 13 times); excluded were more than 20 lifetime uses of hallucinogens or MDMA, illicit drug use in the past 2 months (cannabis excepted), a personal or first-degree family history of major psychiatric disorder and interfering medicines; Basel
lines.exposure: MDMA 100 mg (four 25 mg capsules; analysed 25.40 mg each) and LSD base 100 µg (oral solution; analysed content 92.5 µg) taken at the same time, double-blind and double-dummy, in a calm hospital room with one investigator (study conditions)
lines.comparator: LSD 100 µg alone, MDMA 100 mg alone and placebo in the same people, at least 10 days apart, in block-randomized, counterbalanced order
lines.outcome: Peak blood pressure, heart rate, body temperature and pupil size; complaint scores for 0 to 12 and 12 to 24 hours, self-rated bad drug effect, fear and nausea, and adverse events; blood levels of LSD and MDMA over 24 hours
lines.magnitude: Straumann et al. (2023), 24 people (Table 1, mean ± SEM; placebo, MDMA, LSD, LSD + MDMA; F(3,69); Tukey tests): systolic 124 ± 2.4, 148 ± 2.9, 137 ± 2.7 and 150 ± 2.9 mmHg (combination against LSD p < 0.001, against MDMA not significant); diastolic 77 ± 1.7, 89 ± 1.4, 85 ± 1.8 and 90 ± 1.4 (combination against LSD p < 0.05); mean arterial 92, 107, 102 and 109 (combination against LSD p < 0.001); heart rate 77 ± 2.6, 95 ± 3.4, 92 ± 4.5 and 100 ± 3.6 bpm (combination against LSD p < 0.05, against MDMA not significant); rate-pressure product 9290, 13698, 12385 and 14678 mmHg × bpm (combination against LSD p < 0.001); body temperature 37.0 ± 0.05, 37.3 ± 0.07, 37.4 ± 0.06 and 37.5 ± 0.08 °C (combination against LSD not significant, against MDMA p < 0.05; MDMA against LSD not significant); pupil size 6.0, 7.1, 7.0 and 7.2 mm (combination against LSD p < 0.05; n = 23). Complaints: acute (0–12 h) 1.9 ± 1.1, 8.6 ± 1.8, 15 ± 1.9 and 15 ± 2.2 (combination against LSD not significant); subacute (12–24 h) −0.2 ± 0.5, 2.5 ± 0.9, 3.1 ± 1.0 and 5.5 ± 1.4 (combination against LSD not significant, against MDMA p < 0.05). Visual analogue peaks (% of maximum): bad drug effect 0.2, 6.4, 18 and 14 (combination against LSD not significant); fear 0.2, 2.3, 13 and 8.2 (not significant); nausea 1.0, 7.9, 25 and 21 (MDMA lower than LSD, p < 0.001, and than the combination, p < 0.05; LSD against combination not significant). Blood levels (Table 2, geometric mean, 95% CI; paired t-tests): LSD peak 1.9 (1.7–2.1) alone and 2.1 (1.9–2.3) ng/mL with MDMA (p < 0.05); half-life 3.9 (3.5–4.4) and 5.2 (4.6–5.9) h (p < 0.001); AUC∞ 14 (12–17) and 19 (16–22) ng·h/mL (p < 0.01); apparent clearance 6.9 and 5.3 L/h (p < 0.01); time to peak 1.6 h in both. MDMA peak 233 (215–252) alone and 208 (189–228) ng/mL with LSD (p < 0.001); time to peak 2.8 (2.5–3.2) and 3.5 (3.0–4.0) h (p < 0.01); half-life 8.3 and 8.2 h; AUC∞ 3083 and 3068 ng·h/mL (some MDMA-alone values from 23 people). Editors' calculation from the printed means: LSD AUC∞ about 36% higher, MDMA peak about 11% lower. No severe adverse events.
lines.reasoning: Randomized within-person crossover: starts high (METHODS 6.3). Risk of bias −1 and imprecision −1 give low. The larger blood-pressure and heart-rate rises with both drugs than with LSD alone, objective and significant in the same people, would be rated moderate on their own; the findings on temperature and unwanted effects rest on non-significant tests and are worded as such. Status single study: the first controlled human study of the combination, from one laboratory. The claim leaves out how strong or long the good effects felt, and gives no timing.

lines.q: What if I take LSD and MDMA at the same time?
lines.short: Blood pressure and heart rate went higher than on LSD alone, and bad feelings weren't clearly eased. In a lab study of 24 people, top blood pressure was 13 points higher.
lines.but: Healthy people took one amount of each, in a calm hospital room. Nothing serious happened, but 24 people can't show rare dangers.
how: 24 healthy adults each had four hospital days, at least 10 days apart. They got LSD, MDMA, both at once, or a dummy, in random order and without being told which.

With both, top blood pressure averaged 150, against 137 on LSD alone and 148 on MDMA alone; heart rate 100 beats a minute, against 92 and 95. Body temperature was not clearly higher than on LSD alone.
Bad-feeling, fear and complaint scores were not clearly lower than on LSD alone. Nobody had a serious problem. On nausea, the paper contradicts itself.
The two drugs changed each other's blood levels: more LSD stayed in the blood for longer, while MDMA peaked lower and later.

lines.statement: In the United States, law-enforcement seizure records and overdose death records describe counterfeit pills taking a growing part in fentanyl exposure from 2018 to 2021, comparing the first with the last quarter of each period; neither source tested what share of pills sold on the street contain fentanyl. In quarterly records from the High Intensity Drug Trafficking Areas programme (33 designated trafficking areas, in 50 states and the District of Columbia, whose participating federal, state, local and tribal agencies report their seizures), seizures in which any fentanyl or fentanyl analogue was detected rose between January–March 2018 and October–December 2021 from 424 to 1,539 for powders and from 68 to 635 for pills. Pills were thus 13.8% of these pill-plus-powder fentanyl seizures at the start and 29.2% at the end (68 of 492 and 635 of 2,174, editors' calculation); the authors' conclusion that 'over a quarter of fentanyl seizures are now in pill form' refers to this share of seizures, not to the share of pills that held fentanyl. The number of fentanyl-containing pills seized in a quarter rose from 42,202 to 2,089,186, partly because pill seizures grew larger (about 621 pills per pill seizure at the start and about 3,290 at the end, editors' calculation). Read from the figures, all four counts were higher in April–June or July–September 2021 than in the last quarter, while the pill share was at its highest in the last quarter. The records hold nothing on what the pills were made to look like, how much fentanyl they held, what else they contained or where in the country the changes happened, and seizures reflect policing, testing and reporting as well as supply, which the authors acknowledge (Palamar et al., 2022). In death records from 30 jurisdictions (29 states and the District of Columbia) in CDC's State Unintentional Drug Overdose Reporting System, the share of unintentional or undetermined-intent overdose deaths with evidence of counterfeit pill use was 2.0% in July–September 2019 and 4.7% in October–December 2021 (106,293 deaths over the period), after a high of about 5.1% in April–June 2021 (read from the figure); in the eight western jurisdictions it went from 4.7% to 14.7%, their highest quarter, and it stayed below 4% in the other regions. Evidence of counterfeit pill use meant any of: pills at the scene identified as counterfeit; pills that tested positive for drugs other than what they appeared to contain; pills that looked like oxycodone or alprazolam when that drug was absent on post-mortem toxicology; unmarked pills; or a witness report of pill use when no drug detected exists as a legitimate pill. It was coded from death-investigation narratives; how many pills were tested in a laboratory is not reported; the authors expect it to be undercounted, unevenly within and between jurisdictions; and some pills found at a scene may not have been used. In 2021, in 35 jurisdictions, 2,437 of 54,768 overdose deaths (4.4%) had such evidence: of counterfeit oxycodone only in 1,346 (55.2%; pills marked 'M-30' documented in 889 of them), of counterfeit alprazolam (Xanax) only in 415 (17.0%, editors' calculation), of both in 95 (3.9%) and of an unspecified type in 581 (23.8%, editors' calculation); 55.8% of them were in western jurisdictions, against 16.3% of other overdose deaths.
