Illicitly manufactured fentanyls were listed as a cause of 93.0% of the deaths with such evidence against 72.2% of other overdose deaths, and as the only drugs listed (alcohol not counted) in 41.4% against 19.5%; illicit benzodiazepines in 5.3% against 1.4%, and in 17.1% of the deaths with evidence of counterfeit alprazolam only. These are drugs listed as causes of death, not the contents of tested pills; the authors infer that the pills used likely contained the drugs that caused death (O'Donnell et al., 2023). The one drug-checking study read, at two supervised consumption sites in Vancouver in 2017–2018, tested mostly powders and very few pills (no number given) and reports no results by form, so it gives no figures for pills (Tupper et al., 2018). How well fentanyl test strips detect fentanyl is a separate answer (see the answers on fentanyl test strips). Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
lines.population: Fentanyl-containing drug seizures recorded by law-enforcement agencies taking part in the 33 US High Intensity Drug Trafficking Areas (50 states and the District of Columbia), 2018–2021; unintentional and undetermined-intent drug overdose deaths with a medical examiner or coroner report in 30 US jurisdictions (29 states and the District of Columbia), July 2019 to December 2021, and in 35 jurisdictions in 2021; and samples brought for drug checking at two supervised consumption sites in Vancouver, Canada, 2017–2018
lines.exposure: Pill form, against powder form, among fentanyl-containing seizures; documented evidence of counterfeit pill use among overdose deaths
lines.comparator: The first against the last quarter of each period, with no statistical test of the death-record trend; for 2021, overdose deaths without such evidence in the same jurisdictions; census regions
lines.outcome: Quarterly counts of fentanyl-containing powder and pill seizures, the pill share of pill-plus-powder fentanyl seizures and the number of pills seized; the quarterly share of overdose deaths with evidence of counterfeit pill use, the pill imitated and the drugs listed as causes of death
lines.magnitude: Palamar et al. (2022), HIDTA seizure records, 2018 Q1 against 2021 Q4: fentanyl powder seizures 424 against 1,539 (+263.0%); fentanyl pill seizures 68 against 635 (+833.8%); pill share of pill-plus-powder fentanyl seizures 13.8% against 29.2% (68/492 and 635/2,174, editors' calculation); fentanyl-containing pills seized 42,202 against 2,089,186 (+4,850.4%), about 621 against 3,290 pills per pill seizure (editors' calculation); powder weight 298.2 against 2,416.0 kg (+710.2%). Read from the figures (approximate): powder seizures about 2,050 and pill seizures about 675 at their 2021 Q3 peaks; pills seized about 2.73 million and powder weight about 2,920 kg at their 2021 Q2 peaks; the pill share highest in 2021 Q4. No intervals for the changes; the β coefficients are not defined. O'Donnell et al. (2023), SUDORS, 30 jurisdictions, 106,293 deaths: share with evidence of counterfeit pill use 2.0% (2019 Q3) against 4.7% (2021 Q4), high about 5.1% in 2021 Q2 (read from the figure); West 4.7% against 14.7%; other regions below 4%. 2021, 35 jurisdictions: 2,437 of 54,768 deaths (4.4%); counterfeit oxycodone only 1,346 (55.2%; M-30 pills documented in 889, 66.0%), alprazolam only 415 (17.0%), both 95 (3.9%), unspecified 581 (23.8%) (17.0% and 23.8% editors' calculation); West 55.8% against 16.3% of other deaths; with against without evidence: any illicitly manufactured fentanyl 93.0% against 72.2%, these fentanyls only 41.4% against 19.5%, illicit benzodiazepines 5.3% against 1.4% (17.1% with counterfeit alprazolam only, 18.9% with both, 1.5% with counterfeit oxycodone only). No tests or intervals. Tupper et al. (2018): very few pills tested (no number), no results by form.
lines.reasoning: Descriptive (counts, shares and their change over time in records): starts low, is never upgraded, and is downgraded one level for risk of bias because coverage and measurement could materially change the figures (see the domain note); inconsistency, indirectness as worded, imprecision and publication bias are not downgraded. Very low. Status replicated: two independent record systems, run by different teams, agree in direction (pills became a larger part of US fentanyl seizures in 2018–2021, and deaths with evidence of counterfeit pills a larger share of overdose deaths in 2019–2021); each figure comes from one source, the two measure different things and their sizes cannot be compared, and O'Donnell et al. cite Palamar et al. without sharing its data. Both are compared first quarter against last quarter, and in both the counts or the total share peaked in mid-2021, which the statement says. The drug-checking study qualifies the claim only by showing that it cannot answer for pills. Nothing here measures the share of street pills that contain fentanyl, how much they hold, or the risk of using a counterfeit pill; the DEA laboratory figures on pill contents that Palamar et al. cite were not read and are not used.

lines.q: Are fake pills with fentanyl getting more common?
lines.short: Yes, in US records to 2021. Overdose deaths with signs of fake pills rose from 2 to about 5 in 100, and to about 15 in 100 in western states.
lines.but: Nobody tested what share of street pills hold fentanyl. These are police and death records, and death records likely miss many fake pills.
how: US police records: of seizures that held fentanyl, pills were 14 in 100 in early 2018 and 29 in 100 in late 2021. The rest were powder. Fentanyl pills seized in three months rose from about 42,000 to about 2.1 million.

Death records from 29 states and Washington, DC: deaths with signs of fake pills went from 2 in 100 in mid-2019 to a high of about 5 in 100 in mid-2021, then stayed near there. In western states, about 5 became about 15 in 100.

In 2021, 55 in 100 of these deaths involved fake oxycodone only, often marked 'M-30', and 17 in 100 fake alprazolam (Xanax) only. Fentanyl or similar drugs were among the recorded causes in 93 in 100.
Neither record shows what the pills held: police data have no pill contents, and death records don't say how many pills were tested. A drug-checking study in Vancouver tested too few pills to say.

lines.statement: In 62 people recruited by staff of six US overdose-training and naloxone-distribution programmes in 2005–2006 (in Chicago, New Mexico, San Francisco, Baltimore and two in New York City; 72.6% men, 85.5% currently or formerly using drugs, 22.6% syringe-exchange staff), the 30 trained by the recruiting programme (a median of 8 months before, range 1 to 80 months) compared with the 32 not trained by it were associated with higher scores at recognising opioid overdoses in 16 written scenarios and at deciding when naloxone was called for, scored against the answers of 11 medical experts; trained people still misjudged some opioid overdoses, and both groups often misjudged the scenarios that were not opioid overdoses. The scenarios were experiences that people who inject drugs had described as overdoses in an earlier study; by the experts' combined answers, 9 were opioid overdoses, all calling for naloxone, and 7 were non-opioid overdoses or not overdoses, not calling for it, and respondents could also answer that there was not enough information. Trained respondents recognised on average 7.13 of the 9 opioid overdoses (SD 1.38) against 5.18 (SD 2.55) for untrained respondents (p < 0.001), but 4.63 against 4.28 of the 7 other scenarios (p = 0.42); their totals, 11.77 against 9.47 of 16 (p < 0.005), are 73.6% and 59.2% correct (editors' calculation), not the 85.2% and 68.3% printed in the paper's table and text. Trained respondents chose naloxone in 6.93 of the 9 opioid overdoses against 5.77 (p < 0.05), so on average they did not choose it in about 2 of the 9 against about 3 (2.1 and 3.2 in the paper), and chose it in 0.4 against 1.7 of the 7 scenarios where it was not called for (p < 0.001); naloxone totals were 13.53 against 11.09 of 16 (84.6% and 69.3% correct, p < 0.0001). The experts themselves answered that there was not enough information in 25.6% of their ratings, against 16.0% for trained respondents. The paper reports agreement with the experts as a weighted kappa of 0.85 (95% CI 0.72 to 0.98) for trained and 0.48 (0.18 to 0.77) for untrained respondents, and a kappa of 1.0 for trained respondents' naloxone choices, without saying what was compared; since trained individuals averaged 84.6% correct on naloxone, these figures cannot mean that each trained person matched the experts. All six programmes taught how to tell an opioid overdose from a 'heavy nod', and two explicitly covered non-opioid (for example stimulant) overdoses. The paper gives no results by scenario or by sign and does not print the scenarios, so it cannot show which situations, a heavy nod among them, people got wrong. Programme staff chose who took part and nobody was tested before training, so the difference cannot be credited to training; two of the 11 experts who set the answers are named among the evaluated programmes' staff; the scenarios were written descriptions, not real overdoses; and the paper does not mention fentanyl. The authors' conclusion that 'naloxone training programs are effective and probably cost–effective' rests on this one comparison, with no costs, deaths or real overdoses measured (Green et al., 2008). Whether take-home naloxone programmes lower deaths is a separate answer (see the answer on naloxone programmes). Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
lines.population: People recruited by staff at six US overdose-training and naloxone-distribution programmes (Chicago; State of New Mexico; San Francisco; Baltimore; New York City, two programmes), October 2005 to July 2006: 62 respondents, 72.6% men, 85.5% currently or formerly using drugs, 22.6% syringe-exchange staff
lines.exposure: Having been trained in overdose recognition and response by the recruiting programme (a median of 8 months before; trainings of about 15 to 120 minutes)
lines.comparator: People at the same programmes not trained by them (32); and an answer key from 11 medical experts combined by latent class analysis
lines.outcome: Number of 16 written overdose scenarios correctly classified (opioid overdose, or non-opioid overdose or not an overdose) and correctly judged as calling or not calling for naloxone; agreement with the experts (kappa)
lines.magnitude: Green et al. (2008), trained (n = 30) against untrained (n = 32), mean (SD): opioid overdoses recognised 7.13 (1.38) against 5.18 (2.55) of 9, t60 = −3.76, P < 0.001; other scenarios 4.63 (1.40) against 4.28 (1.94) of 7, P = 0.42; recognition total 11.77 (1.92) against 9.47 (3.48) of 16, P < 0.005 (73.6% against 59.2%, editors' calculation; printed as 85.2% against 68.3%); naloxone chosen in opioid overdoses 6.93 (1.76) against 5.77 (2.30) of 9, P < 0.05 (not chosen in 2.1 against 3.2); naloxone correctly not chosen 6.60 (0.72) against 5.32 (1.94) of 7, P < 0.001 (chosen where not called for in 0.4 against 1.7); naloxone total 13.53 (1.96) against 11.09 (2.32) of 16 (84.6% against 69.3%), P < 0.0001. 'Not enough information' in 25.6% of the experts' ratings against 16.0% of trained respondents'. Weighted kappa with the experts 0.85 (0.72–0.98) trained, 0.48 (0.18–0.77) untrained; naloxone kappa 1.0 trained, 0.75 (0.44–1.0) untrained (unit of comparison not stated).
lines.reasoning: Observational (a non-randomized comparison of trained and untrained people at one time): starts low; risk of bias −1 (see the domain note); inconsistency, indirectness as worded, imprecision and publication bias 0. Very low. Status single study: no other study of how well people recognise overdose scenarios was read. The claim is worded as an association between having been trained and scores on written scenarios; whether training causes better recognition, how people do at real overdoses, which signs they miss and whether training changes deaths or costs are not shown by this design. The paper's printed recognition percentages do not match its means, and its kappa of 1.0 cannot describe individuals; the statement gives the means and says so. Research findings only: the claim names no signs to look for and no steps to take, which belong to the senior author's emergency guidance (METHODS §8).

lines.q: Would I know if someone was overdosing on opioids?
lines.short: Not always. On a written test, people trained by overdose programmes spotted about 7 of 9 opioid overdoses. People without that training spotted about 5 of 9.
lines.but: It was a paper test with 62 people that staff picked, not real overdoses. Nobody was tested before training, so training may not be the reason.
how: In 2005 and 2006, 62 people at six US overdose programmes read 16 short stories. Each was based on what someone who injects drugs had called an overdose. Medical experts had decided 9 were opioid overdoses needing naloxone, and 7 were not.
Trained people spotted about 7 of the 9 opioid overdoses, untrained people about 5. Trained people still didn't choose naloxone in about 2 of the 9; untrained people missed about 3.
Both groups got only about 4 or 5 of the other 7 stories right. Even the experts said there wasn't enough information in about a quarter of their answers.
The paper doesn't say which stories people got wrong. So it can't show which signs get missed, or whether people can tell a heavy nod from an overdose.

lines.statement: In people who use heroin, evidence is insufficient to say whether taking it in surroundings not linked with past use raises the risk of overdose: the idea comes from a conditioning model of tolerance tested mainly in rats, and the only study in people is a set of 10 overdose survivors' recollections with no comparison. The model, as its author states it (Siegel, 1984, 2005): cues present when a drug is taken, such as the place, the people and the act of taking it, become linked with its effects and come to trigger responses that oppose those effects; these learned responses are part of tolerance, so tolerance should be weaker where the drug has not been taken before. The animal evidence is described by the same author without figures: rats with the same heroin history were more likely to survive a high intravenous dose given in the environment previously paired with heroin than the same dose given in a different environment (Siegel et al., 1982, as described in Siegel, 1984; the 1982 paper itself was not read), and setting-specific tolerance is said to have been seen for a variety of effects, lethal effects included, of various drugs in many species (Siegel, 2005, citing his group's 2000 review, with no study, species or figure named). The 2005 review also describes, without numbers, two laboratory examples in people that do not involve opioids: more tolerance to alcohol drunk in a familiar beer-flavoured drink than in an unfamiliar blue, peppermint-flavoured one, and more tolerance to a heart effect of caffeine taken in coffee than at the same blood level reached intravenously. The only human study of overdose: 10 people formerly dependent on heroin (8 men, 2 women; mean age 28), attending one methadone maintenance clinic in the New York City area and each with a hospital admission for overdose in their records, were asked to recount the occasion on average 5 years later; 7 described something unusual: 2 had injected in places where they had never injected before, 1 had used for the first time in his own living room, with a large group at his wedding celebration, and alone overdosed from the shared supply, 2 described an unusual injection, 1 had taken a barbiturate mixture with the heroin against his usual practice, and 1 had injected heroin without the cocaine he usually took with it; 3 recalled nothing distinctive (Siegel, 1984). An unfamiliar place or company was thus recalled by 3 of the 10 (editors' count). There was no comparison with these people's ordinary occasions of use or with people who did not overdose, the accounts were sorted by the author without stated definitions, and only survivors were interviewed, although the abstract extends the suggestion to overdose deaths; the author states that the reports do not prove a conditioning mechanism, that large doses and drug combinations also contribute, that the barbiturate case may be a drug interaction, and that how often people use heroin in unusual circumstances without harm is unknown. The 2005 review presents no data on overdose in people and does not cite the interviews; it proposes a form of cue-exposure treatment (meeting drug cues without the drug, so that the learned responses fade) that also includes internal cues, and cites no trial of it. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
lines.population: People who use heroin: in the only human study, 10 people formerly dependent on heroin, in methadone maintenance at one clinic in the New York City area, each with a hospital admission for overdose in their records (8 men, 2 women; mean age 28 at interview), interviewed on average 5 years after the overdose; in the animal work the model's author describes, rats and other species
lines.exposure: Taking an opioid in surroundings, company or circumstances not previously linked with taking it (in the human study, anything the person recalled as unusual on the overdose occasion: an unfamiliar place or company, an unusual injection, an unusual drug combination or the absence of a usual one)
lines.comparator: None in the human study (no comparison with the same people's ordinary occasions of use or with people who did not overdose); in the rat experiment, the same final dose given in the environment previously paired with heroin, to rats with the same heroin history
lines.outcome: Overdose (hospital-treated, survivors only) in people; in animals, tolerance and death after a high dose
lines.magnitude: Siegel (1984): 7 of 10 survivors described the circumstances of the overdose occasion as unusual (70%; exact 95% CI 35% to 93%, editors' calculation): 2 injected in places where they had never injected before; 1 used in his own living room, where he had never taken heroin, with a large group at his wedding celebration, and alone overdosed from the shared supply; 2 described unusual injection procedures; 1 took a barbiturate mixture with heroin against his usual practice; 1 injected heroin without the cocaine he usually combined with it, for the first time in over 9 months; 3 of 10 recalled no distinctive feature. Unfamiliar place or company: 3 of 10 (editors' count). No comparison group, no comparison occasions, no test. Rat experiment (Siegel et al., 1982), as described by its author: rats given a high intravenous heroin dose in the environment previously paired with heroin were more likely to survive than rats with the same history given it in a different environment; no survival figures given. Siegel (2005): no sample size or effect size for any study it cites.
lines.reasoning: The only human evidence on overdose and setting is a case series of 10 survivors' recollections with no comparison (Siegel, 1984): observational, starts low; down two levels for risk of bias, one for indirectness and one for imprecision; very low. The model and the animal findings come from the same author, described without figures in a short narrative review (Siegel, 2005) and in the 1984 paper's introduction; they show why the idea is plausible and are labelled as animal findings, but they are not evidence about people and do not raise the rating. The 1982 rat experiment itself was not read: the PDF saved under its name is a copy of the 1984 paper. Relation: insufficient evidence, because no study of people compared overdose occasions with ordinary ones. Status: single study (one human study; the 2005 review adds no human overdose data and does not cite it).

lines.q: Can using in a new place make an overdose more likely?
lines.short: Maybe. In rats, heroin was more often deadly in a new place. In people, nobody has tested it well. One study asked 10 overdose survivors what was different.
lines.but: That's 10 people's memories, about 5 years later, with nobody to compare them with. Only 3 of them recalled a new place or crowd.
how: The idea: the place, the people and the ritual that come with a drug start to trigger the body's push-back against it. That push-back is part of tolerance, so it may be weaker somewhere new.
In rat studies from the same researcher, tolerance was weaker in a new place, and a large dose of heroin was more often deadly there. Rats aren't people.
Of 10 overdose survivors, 7 recalled something unusual that day: 3 a new place or crowd, 2 a different way of injecting, 2 a different mix of drugs. The other 3 recalled nothing unusual.
Nobody counted how often people use somewhere new without an overdose. The review suggests a treatment based on the idea, but cites no test of it.

lines.statement: As described in one editorial, with figures second-hand and cases gathered without a search, deaths during opioid withdrawal have been reported, all of them in custody, but the evidence is insufficient to say how often withdrawal leads to death, whether such deaths are increasing, or what the risk is outside custody. The editorial, by three researchers in Sydney, says that opioid withdrawal is generally seen as a flu-like illness, subjectively severe but objectively mild, unlike alcohol and benzodiazepine withdrawal, which it calls life-threatening, and that death is uncommon but does occur (Darke et al., 2017). Its proposed mechanism: persistent vomiting and diarrhoea, if untreated, can lead to dehydration, raised blood sodium (hypernatraemia) and resulting heart failure. Its cases: a woman in custody in the United Kingdom in 1998 who went into heroin withdrawal with persistent vomiting, sudden weight loss and dehydration and died of brain damage from lack of oxygen after a cardiac arrest, a death for which a failure of the duty of care was argued successfully before the European Court of Human Rights; and 10 deaths in United States jails reported in the press between 2013 and 2016 that the authors were aware of (six women and four men, aged 18 to 49), listed in an online appendix that was not read. The authors judge every such death preventable with appropriate medical care, say that in each case the process of dying appeared prolonged, with ample time to treat, and describe the deaths as neglect or a lack of medical resources; they cite one survey in which only a quarter of US jails had alcohol or drug detoxification services. The editorial gives no rate and no number of people going through withdrawal, and its statement that the number of withdrawal deaths in US jails is rising comes without counts over time; the cases come from press reports and a court case, so deaths that were not reported, or not attributed to withdrawal, are missed, and the text does not describe the cases' causes of death beyond the UK case, their medical histories or other drugs involved, including withdrawal from alcohol or benzodiazepines. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
lines.population: People going through opioid withdrawal in custody (jails and prisons in the United Kingdom and the United States), as described in one editorial
lines.exposure: Opioid withdrawal (from heroin and other opioids) without adequate medical management
lines.comparator: None (reported cases; no comparison group and no denominator)
lines.outcome: Death during withdrawal, as reported in the press and in a court case (causes as the editorial gives them)
lines.magnitude: No rate or denominator. Darke et al. (2017), second-hand: 1 death in UK custody (1998); 10 press-reported deaths in US jails, 2013–2016 (6 women, 4 men, aged 18 to 49; listed in an appendix not read). Second-hand figure: a quarter of US jails in one survey (Fiscella et al., 2004) had alcohol or drug detoxification services.
lines.reasoning: The evidence is reported cases, seen only through an editorial: a claim seen only through reviews starts from the design of the studies they describe (METHODS 6.3), here observational case reports, so it starts low; down for risk of bias (unsystematic cases that cannot be appraised), indirectness (second-hand; custody only) and imprecision (no denominator); very low. Every supporting anchor is the editorial (narrative-review design on its card), so the claim stays at draft and says in its statement that its figures are second-hand (METHODS 6.3). Relation: insufficient evidence on how often withdrawal kills; the statement says only that deaths have been reported, as the editorial describes them. Status: single study (one editorial).

lines.q: Can opioid withdrawal itself kill you?
lines.short: It has happened, but nobody knows how often. One editorial lists 11 deaths, all in jail. It links them to vomiting and diarrhoea that dried people out and went untreated.
lines.but: It's one editorial's list, built from news reports and a court case. With no count of how many people went through withdrawal, there's no rate.
how: The authors' idea: vomiting and diarrhoea that don't stop, left untreated, dry the body out. Blood sodium rises, and the heart can fail.
The cases: a woman in custody in the UK in 1998, and 10 people in US jails reported in the press from 2013 to 2016, aged 18 to 49.
The authors say each death came slowly, with time to treat it, and call the deaths neglect or a lack of medical care.
They say such deaths are rising but give no counts over time. Nothing here covers withdrawal outside custody.

lines.statement: In people with opioid dependence who entered methadone maintenance treatment in high-income countries, periods out of treatment were associated with higher death rates than periods in treatment, with the highest rates in the first four weeks after leaving; three buprenorphine cohorts showed a similar but less certain pattern. A systematic review pooled 19 cohorts published 1974–2016 (18 methadone cohorts, 122,885 people, followed 1965–2010; 3 buprenorphine cohorts, 15,831 people, 1990–2010; 11 in Europe or Israel, 4 in North America, 4 in Australia), counting time in and out of treatment for the same people (Sordo et al., 2017). With methadone, the pooled all-cause death rate was 11.3 per 1,000 person-years in treatment (95% CI 8.4 to 15.2) and 36.1 out of treatment (24.5 to 53.3), an unadjusted difference of 24.9 (13.6 to 36.1) and a ratio of 3.20 (2.65 to 3.86), in 16 cohorts; every cohort had a higher rate out of treatment (cohort rates 5.1 to 39.5 in treatment and 12.4 to 130.2 out). These pooled figures are random-effects averages across very different cohorts (I² 98%): in the three largest, recent register cohorts, which hold 83% of the person-years, the differences were 5.5 to 11.2 and the ratios 1.8 to 2.7, and adding up all deaths and person-years gives 7.1 against 16.4 (editors' calculations from the per-cohort figures). Overdose deaths with methadone (11 cohorts) were 2.6 (2.1 to 3.3) in treatment against 12.7 (6.9 to 23.4) out, a difference of 10.0 (2.6 to 17.4) and a ratio of 4.80 (2.90 to 7.96), higher out of treatment in every cohort. By time since starting or leaving methadone (five recent cohorts, after the review left out one cohort of people with HIV who inject; one cohort split at two weeks instead of four), the rate was 11.4 (5.8 to 22.4) in the first four weeks of treatment against 5.8 (5.0 to 6.7) for the rest of treatment, a ratio of 1.97 (0.94 to 4.10) that was not statistically significant; and 32.1 (19.1 to 53.9) in the first four weeks after leaving against 13.5 (11.9 to 15.3) for the rest of the time out of treatment, a difference of 18.6 (2.9 to 34.3) and a ratio of 2.38 (1.51 to 3.74), higher in the first period in each of the five cohorts; the review did not compare the weeks after leaving with time in treatment directly. The rise after leaving was seen in deaths from all causes: in the three methadone cohorts that gave overdose deaths by period, the overdose rate was 4.2 (1.8 to 9.9) in the first four weeks after leaving against 3.4 (2.3 to 5.1) later, from 20 overdose deaths in the first period, and in the two cohorts that gave both counts, 18 of the 79 deaths in the first four weeks after leaving were counted as overdoses (editors' count and calculation); the authors expect overdose deaths to be undercounted and note that deaths from suicide and injury are also more common in that period. With buprenorphine (3 cohorts; 96% of the deaths from Australian studies), the rate was 4.3 (2.1 to 8.9) in treatment against 9.5 (3.9 to 23.4) out (difference 5.2, −1.0 to 11.4; ratio 2.20, 1.34 to 3.61), 4.5 both in the first four weeks and in the rest of treatment, and 32.0 (13.2 to 77.5) in the first four weeks after leaving against 10.9 (8.5 to 13.9) later (two cohorts; difference 21.2, −5.9 to 48.2). All pooled estimates are unadjusted; in the cohorts that reported ratios adjusted for demographics, severity of drug use, treatment or illness (five methadone and one buprenorphine cohort for all causes), the ratios were unchanged or larger. But people leave and re-enter treatment for reasons that may themselves affect their risk; the review had no data on why people left or on tolerance or drug use after leaving, and its results do not separate people who finished a planned reduction from people who dropped out or were discharged; people lost to follow-up may be at higher risk; medicines obtained outside treatment were not captured; and people in prison or recently released, in detoxification or never treated were excluded. The authors suggest that loss of tolerance, assuming many people return to use, and the use of several substances may explain the rise after leaving. The discussion's statement that death rates were significantly lower with buprenorphine than with methadone has no test or estimate in the results. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
lines.population: People with opioid dependence who entered methadone maintenance (18 cohorts, 122,885 people, follow-up 1965–2010) or buprenorphine maintenance (3 cohorts, 15,831 people, 1990–2010) in 19 cohorts from high-income countries (11 Europe or Israel, 4 North America, 4 Australia); people in prison or recently released, in detoxification or other treatments, and never-treated people excluded
lines.exposure: Periods out of methadone or buprenorphine maintenance treatment after leaving it, for any reason, with the first four weeks after leaving shown separately; and the first four weeks after starting treatment
lines.comparator: Periods in treatment in the same cohorts (for the interval analyses, the rest of the time in treatment after the first four weeks, and the rest of the time out of treatment after the first four weeks); crude, unadjusted comparisons
lines.outcome: Crude all-cause and overdose death rates per 1,000 person-years, from cohort records and population mortality registers
lines.magnitude: Sordo et al. (2017), pooled crude rates per 1,000 person-years (bivariate random effects; unadjusted). Methadone, all causes (16 cohorts): in treatment 11.3 (95% CI 8.4 to 15.2), out 36.1 (24.5 to 53.3); difference 24.9 (13.6 to 36.1); ratio 3.20 (2.65 to 3.86); I² 98%; cohort rates in 5.1 to 39.5, out 12.4 to 130.2, higher out in all 16; leaving out one cohort at a time 10.6 to 11.9 in and 32.5 to 39.1 out. Editors' calculations from Fig 2: three largest cohorts (Degenhardt 2009, Evans 2015, Kimber 2015; 83% of person-years) differences 8.5, 11.2 and 5.5, ratios 2.5, 2.7 and 1.8; all deaths over all person-years 7.1 in against 16.4 out (ratio 2.3). Methadone, overdose (11 cohorts): 2.6 (2.1 to 3.3) against 12.7 (6.9 to 23.4); difference 10.0 (2.6 to 17.4); ratio 4.80 (2.90 to 7.96); I² 66% in and 97% out; higher out in all 11 (editors' reading of Fig 3). Methadone by interval (5 cohorts; Degenhardt 2009 split at two weeks): first four weeks in treatment 11.4 (5.8 to 22.4) against 5.8 (5.0 to 6.7) later in treatment, difference 5.6 (−2.4 to 13.6), ratio 1.97 (0.94 to 4.10); first four weeks after leaving 32.1 (19.1 to 53.9) against 13.5 (11.9 to 15.3) later out, difference 18.6 (2.9 to 34.3), ratio 2.38 (1.51 to 3.74); higher in the first period after leaving in each cohort (20.0 against 14.2 to 57.6 against 15.3). Trend analysis: fitted rate falling from 37.4 to 6.4 over the first four weeks of methadone treatment; 24.1 to 35.2 over the first two weeks after leaving, then declining (non-linearity P = 0.04). Overdose by interval, methadone (3 cohorts): in treatment 3.5 (1.3 to 9.5) against 2.0 (1.5 to 2.7); out 4.2 (1.8 to 9.9) against 3.4 (2.3 to 5.1); 20 overdose deaths in the first four weeks out (editors' count from Fig 6); in Kimber 2015 and Cousins 2016, 10 of 35 and 8 of 44 deaths in the first four weeks after leaving were counted as overdoses, 18 of 79 (editors' calculation from Figs 4 and 6, same person-years). Buprenorphine, all causes (3 cohorts): 4.3 (2.1 to 8.9) against 9.5 (3.9 to 23.4); difference 5.2 (−1.0 to 11.4); ratio 2.20 (1.34 to 3.61); by interval (2 cohorts) 4.5 in both treatment periods; first four weeks after leaving 32.0 (13.2 to 77.5) against 10.9 (8.5 to 13.9), difference 21.2 (−5.9 to 48.2), ratio 2.94 (1.34 to 6.46); overdose (1 cohort) 1.4 against 4.6, and 10.8 against 4.2 out of treatment by interval. Adjusted ratios (Table 4): all causes, methadone, unchanged in two cohorts and 15.5% to 35.5% larger in three; buprenorphine 16.8% larger in one; overdose unchanged in three methadone cohorts and 25.8% and 28.6% larger in two.
lines.reasoning: Cohort studies are observational and start low; downgraded one level for risk of bias because the claim is seen only through one review, rated critically low, and the cohorts themselves were not read (METHODS §6.3, claims seen only through reviews): very low. Not downgraded further: the review prints each cohort's data, the direction holds in all 16 methadone cohorts for all causes and all 11 for overdose, and adjustment in six cohorts left the ratios unchanged or larger. The start of methadone treatment (not statistically significant), the buprenorphine figures (three cohorts, mostly one Australian study) and the overdose figures by period (three cohorts) are worded as uncertain and not rated separately. Whether treatment prevents deaths, or stopping causes them, is not claimed. Status: replicated (16 methadone cohorts from different countries and teams, same direction); one review read.

lines.q: Is it dangerous to stop methadone or buprenorphine (Suboxone)?
lines.short: The weeks after leaving were the riskiest. In 5 studies, deaths in the first 4 weeks off methadone ran at about 32 a year per 1,000 people, against 6 in steady treatment.
lines.but: These studies counted everyone who left, for any reason. People who leave differ in other ways, so the studies can't show that stopping itself caused the deaths.
how: In 16 groups of people on methadone, about 11 in 1,000 died each year in treatment, against about 36 out of it. Every group had more deaths out of treatment.
In the biggest recent groups the gap was smaller: about 6 or 7 deaths a year per 1,000 people in treatment, against 12 to 18 out of it.
Deaths in the first 4 weeks off methadone ran at about 32 a year per 1,000 people, against about 14 later on. The first month on methadone looked riskier too, but that could be chance.
Deaths counted as overdoses didn't clearly rise after leaving, in the 3 groups that split them by time. Buprenorphine had just three groups, mostly one Australian study.
